speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
I should like to finish my review of the activities of the department and my reference to the army in Canada and the various groups into which that army is divided. On Friday I gave particulars of the operational troops and mentioned that they had been considerably reduced as a result of the changed strategic situation and the disbandment of the seventh and eighth divisions.
I also gave the committee some details of the non-operational troops, which are the servicing units and the servicing personnel, not only for Canada but for overseas. There are two further groups I should speak of. One is the training stream, which is tremendously important, and the other is the reselective and disposal stream, or depots as we call them. In the training stream, as of only a few days ago, we had something over 75,000 personnel, of which a little over 15,000-
What is meant by training stream?

That is a stream or group into which men go for training in progressive sequence. They go first to basic training, then to advanced training, then to special arm training, then to the training brigade and then overseas. In personnel, those not actually attached to units, we have something over
75,000.
Not all are in that stream; some do not go overseas?

A little over 15,000 are N.R.M.A. personnel. Regarding the depots or disposal and reselective stream, I am sorry to have to say that the number in these depots has increased. I do not know of any group which is more difficult to regulate than the group in the depots. To the depots come those who are on their way out for discharge, those who have been in a unit which has been disbanded and who have not yet been posted to some other unit, those who come from a unit or a training centre, posted for the time being to the depots until they go to a new job. Generally speaking these depots perform the function of employment agencies for soldiers who are temporarily not posted, either because of unfitness for the job they have had or for which they have been training, or because their unit has been disbanded.
Another function of the depots is the documenting and medical examination and taking care of soldiers who are being discharged.

Is it fair to say that it is a distribution centre?
War Appropriation-Army

I should think so. It is a distribution centre. I suggested that it was more or less a transient hotel for soldiers, but the department sat down on that title definitely. They said it was no such thing, that it is a place where men are actually posted to different unite, where training is done and where every endeavour is made to make the stay at that particular place just as short as possible.

Has there been any
change in the functioning of the depots since the war started?

There has been a great deal more in the way of employment activity. More attention is being paid to selecting men for particular jobs, especially in the last year. As a matter of fact, we have at the depots placement officers similar to those of the Department of Labour. These men are there for the purpose of finding out the jobs in the different districts for which men are wanted, and also looking for men who can best fill those jobs.
Is that the only reason for the increase in the numbers at the depots?
No; the increase in numbers is due to no small extent to the disbandment of the seventh and eighth divisions.
And men returning from overseas, like the forestry corps?

And men returning from overseas. They have to be discharged and the depots have been under additional pressure this year. I am convinced that generally speaking there has been an extra effort put forward to deal with these cases just as fast as possible. There may be some exceptions, but speaking generally those in charge of the depots are never satisfied with the progress being made. I know they are seeking honestly and sincerely for improvement in administration. We endeavour to terminate as speedily as possible the uncertainty which faces a man when he goes to the depot.
I have referred to the placement officers and stated that they fulfil the same function as the placement officers of the Department of Labour in the employment offices. Arrangements have been made to have representatives of the Department of Pensions and National Health at the depots to look after men for whom rehabilitation treatment is needed. That is to say, in connection with men on the way out an endeavour is being made to integrate the services rendered by the Department of Pensions and National Health with the services

rendered by the Department of National Defence. I am sure that hon. members have in their minds cases-there may have been a number of them-in which men seem to get out of the army and not into the Department of Pensions and National Health as promptly as possible. I can only say that both the Minister of Pensions and National Health and I have been constantly at work on that. We have tried to impress our officers with the importance of setting up a system whereby the men will be informed not only by the department of pensions but also by the army of what their rights are; and vice versa. The department of pensions will give to the man who is in the army, even though he has not been discharged, such information as can be given with regard to his rights eventually when he comes to be discharged. That is not merely his right as to pension but as to treatment, vocational allowance, unemployment allowance and all the different benefits provided under the department of pensions. Those depots will become more important as the war goes on and demobilization increases, because the problems of the post-war employment of soldiers will be first encountered and dealt with there. The depots will be the focal point.
Speaking generally with regard to the army in Canada, everybody wants to see it reduced and wonders why it is so large. I wish to speak of two or three features of administration of the army in Canada. We have endeavoured to make some genuine effort to reduce it. In this I point out, if it is any comfort to us, that we are at least as far advanced in this matter as our good neighbours to the south, and in some instances that I know of we took the steps considerably earlier than They did.
What is the total number as of this date?
The total number of what?
Of the home army.

I am going to summarize just as soon as I get through with these reductions. Hon. Mr. Stimson, Secretary of State for War in the United States, only a few days ago issued a statement in which he forecast what he called a drastic shake-up in the army in the United States. He spoke of comb-outs that were being made, of discharges and replacements of physically fit men by men less physically fit. I read his statement with a great deal of interest, and I think I can say that the policies which Mr. Stimson announced

War Appropriation-Army
are along the line of the policies which have been in force in the Canadian army for some time.

The cases are scarcely
parallel.

Yes, they are. Let me
give one or two examples. Our neighbours to the south are replacing physically fit men by members of the Women's Army Corps, soldiers unfit for service overseas, new recruits physically handicapped1 and short-term' enlisted men. Canada releases her physically fit men by utilizing general service personnel returned from overseas, general service personnel unfit for operational duties, the Canadian Women's Army Corps and N.R.M.A. personnel who cannot be absorbed in operational units. That was the great objective-to release men for operational service.
Mr. Stimson mentioned also that they were releasing overhead personnel, which. I take to be those in the non-operational units, which I spoke of the other day as servicing units. In Canada we have been doing exactly the same thing. We have been combing out general service personnel, physically fit. I stated last year that in Canada over sixty per cent of the general service personnel in the non-operational units were men who were below category "A" or over thirty-five years of age. That meant that a comb-out had already taken place. To-day this figure is close to seventy per cent.
Our drive was also to release general service men from operational units in two ways, by comb-out and by disbandment, with the result that during the present fiscal year, ending March 31, 1944, we shall have released probably 15,000 general service personnel from operational units, a large number of whom will be for overseas service.
Mr. Stimson mentioned another feature of the drastic shake-up in the United States, and that was the reverting to inactive status of thousands of commissioned officers over thirty-eight years of age for whom no suitable assignments were available. In that case also we can say that Canada is, to say the least, not behind the United States. Since last September we have had released numbers of officers who could not be suitably employed. We have not fixed a definite age limit in this respect. We have said that they shall be reverted to reserve status if they cannot be advantageously employed in the service in their present rank, and that is regardless of age, whereas in the United States apparently the general policy is limited to deal with officers who are over thirty-eight years of age.
In addition, the Canadian army some months ago inaugurated the retirement age limit; the retirement of officers who it is found cannot
be advantageously employed as well as those who have reached the age ceiling is not a particularly agreeable task. Those who have given good service are naturally anxious to see the war through; but it is obvious, when the peak of expansion is passed, that it is unwise in the interests of both the officer and the service, as well as in the interests of national economy, to continue in active status officers for whom no suitable employment is available or who have reached1 the age limit fixed. We have thought and still think-and it is working out that way-that it affords to the officer an opportunity to reestablish himself in civil life before the rush of demobilization comes. It also gives the younger officer a chance to make his mark in this war. The Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) expressed the same idea in announcing a somewhat similar policy for the air force a few days ago-that it would make the air force more dynamic, vital and virile. That is exactly what it does in the army, under the policies which we inaugurated some time ago.
Is experience no factor?

I want the committee to
follow along with me, if members will permit me to proceed; but I am glad1 that my hon. friend interrupted with that particular question. I can say to my hon. friend that there is just one exception with regard to the retirement of officers of sixty years and over. The officer must be retired unless the adjutant-general certifies that no other suitable officer is available to take the job he is holding, and in that case there may be an extension for one year.
Has the minister the figures on retirements?

I am reaching in the air
for this figure. They have not been completed but I think we have in prospect something like 700. I am not saying 700 over age, but either over age or not advantageously employable in their present rank.
The third advantage is that it promotes efficiency in the service by increasing interest and enthusiasm by the enlargement of opportunity to the younger officers. The fourth advantage is that it releases for civilian occupation men who have had an established place in civil life and who can contribute much toward reconstruction in the transition period. I want to record here what I have already said publicly, namely the appreciation of the department of the services of those older officers and particularly those who served in the last war, who have relinquished their
War Appropriation-Army

civilian occupations without thought of personal sacrifice, and made a fine contribution in this war to help build up the Canadian army of to-day. Those men have done their bit and have now left the army better for their work. Their service is appreciated and they now are giving younger men whom they have helped to train an opportunity to advance.
Mr. Stimson announced also the putting of training camps, stations and other installations on a stand-by basis. We have done the same thing in Canada.
What do you mean by that?

Closing training centres, due to the fact that the peak of expansion was past and that the development of the armed forces was on a maintenance rather than on a capital basis. It is just the same as in connection with our munitions production. That was driven to a peak in order to get production and initial equipment for the formations. That equipment is now in very many cases being produced on a maintenance basis; that is, on a replacement or reinforcement basis. It has not to be furnished initially for further capital formations. We in Canada announced the same policy. That policy applied to both officers' training centres and to other ranks' training centres as well. Last spring I announced the closing down of officers' training centres at Gordon Head and Three Rivers, with the concentration of training at the officers' training centre at Brock-ville. That reduced' overhead and output. We had put forth an aggressive effort to build up the officer strength of the army, which during the days of 1942 was considered very necessary, and was demanded to meet the emergency that developed as a result of events following Pearl Harbor. Our officer strength was built up just as fast as it could be. We have now a reserve. There were two major factors which contributed to that; first, the improvement of conditions which warranted the disbandment of the seventh and eighth divisions making those officers available for other duties; second, the fact that operations in 1943 were not of the degree of intensity for which provision was made. The fact that we are in this comfortable position of having a reserve to meet officer requirements does not mean that officer training has ceased, or that those now serving in the ranks will have no opportunity for commissions. But the general policy is that recommendations for commissions will be made after a man has an opportunity of proving himself overseas rather than in Canada.

We have this reserve of officers, and we are utilizing it by making good use of the time and facilities which we have to broaden and to intensify their training; in other words, adding to their qualifications by giving to them refresher and advanced training to make them just that much more fit to undertake the responsibilitiqs which devolve upon commissioned officers. As I say, we have those facilities, and we are taking advantage of them to give these young officers training far in advance of what would have been possible in the last war.
Mr. Stimson did not speak particularly of officer training alone. He spoke of training camps, stations and other facilities, which would be placed on a stand-by basis. We have done the same thing with regard to our basic training centres.
May I ask one question? Have you brought instructors back from the fighting fronts, such as Sicily, Italy and North Africa, to the officer training centres?

From time to time, yes. I cannot recall names at the moment; we. are bringing them back from time to time. My hon. friend probably heard an officer by the name of Lieutenant Colonel Garneau on the radio last night. Lieutenant Colonel Garneau had been at Sicily and Dieppe and is in Canada now in connection with training.
So far I have spoken about officer training centres. I shall now speak about training camps and other ranks. This is another policy which we have had in force for a considerable time. I have not the date, but as I remember it, it was sometime last summer that I announced the policy of closing several of the training centres and the inauguration of a plan for linking up the basic training with the advanced so that men in a certain basic training centre would know they would be going to the advanced training centre and would not be distributed all over Canada. This made for liaison between centres. The officers in these linked centres knew what the conditions were in the centres with which they were associated and the proficiency which had been arrived at, and the general scope and quality of the training. That is to say, the advanced training centre would know all about the basic training centre, and therefore would be able to pick the man up in his training from where he had left off. It made for more speed and more efficiency than would be the case if the man had come from some basic training centre which the advanced centre did not know.

Why was there such a wide distribution in the early days?

War Appropriation-Army

Simply because they had to be put wherever they could be accommodated. The purpose of reducing the basic training centres and providing the link with the advanced training centre was to reduce overhead and to integrate basic and advanced training.
Since that time thirteen basic training centres have been discontinued and the capacity of eleven more has been reduced. This has permitted a reduction of staff. Some of the closed centres are in use for other purposes and others are on a stand-by basis so that the original capacity can easily be utilized if occasion should arise. In the meantime we have ample basic training capacity for the number of men we assume we estimate we shall require. The closing of the centres where only small numbers were in attendance, and the concentration in fewer establishments has helped the staffs in the training centres to do better work, and the staffs at the districts and at headquarters to give closer and more helpful supervision.

The
training centre at Edmundston is very small; has it been closed?

I do not know; I am not quite sure; I do not think it has.
I should now like to answer the question of the hon. member from Cumberland (Mr. Black), with regard to the army in Canada. Last year I said there would be a definite reduction in the number of troops in Canada. I said that would be largely effected by the dispatch overseas of units already earmarked for overseas service, and of some required for administrative service; that is to say, there would be a reduction by taking units which were in Canada and sending them overseas. The number in Canada earmarked for overseas at that time was about 11,000. As a matter of fact I said that the minimum reduction would be 15,000, I think. I also said that the strength as of March 31st would likely be about 235,000. I am glad to say, on the record we have, that I believe we have done very much better than that. We estimate that the army in Canada will be something over 215,000, as against 235,000 which I predicted last year; that is the active effective strength. We estimate that the reduction, instead of being about 15,000, will be nearer 35,000. Indeed, in the reduction are some 8,000 granted longterm-leave in agriculture, mining and industry who ought not to be charged to the army, since they are only nominally soldiers and have been on leave for months and months. We cannot treat them as soldiers and at the same time have them used in the national economy for something other than military
service. It might be said that we had men on leave last year, but we had very few last year as compared with this year.
Are they included in the 215,000?	'

I think the 8,000 are included in the 35,000 reduction. I should say also the C.W.A.C.'s were not included last year and were not included this year either, but there has been an increase of between three and four thousand in the Canadian Women's Army Corps this year. That increase is not counted in estimating the reduction. To me, the most satisfactory feature of the reduction is that in the process over 70,000 men will have been sent overseas by March 31 of this year.
What about those who have come back and are at the dispersal centres? I refer to the 2,000 foresters. Where do you put these; they are in Canada but are not being used.
I shall give my hon. friend the distribution of the 2,000 foresters. I have not it here. They are being used. Some of them are still at the depots, and if they are there-
It is so small, it is ridiculous.
No, my hon. friend is wrong. There were something like 2,000.
A good many of them have been disbanded.
I will give the distribution.
That was the greatest fiasco of the whole thing.
Will the minister break down those figures?

Under the uncertainties that have existed and the administrative difficulties involved in reorganization, that record of reduction is one in which the department has a right to take some satisfaction. I would remind the committee that included in these figures for" Canada are forces maintained by us on the outposts of the continent, in Newfoundland and Labrador, and in the Caribbean. Included in the figures are the
5,000	sent to Kiska. The break-down as at March 31, 1944, shows that we estimate the operational troops will be over 55,000,. the nonoperational troops something over 75,000, and those in training and awaiting disposal, something over 75,000. The total will be over
215,000.
War Appropriation-Army
Did the minister say that the non-operational troops exceed the operational?
Yes.
Comb them out; that is all I have to say.

My hon. friend does not appreciate what the non-operational troops are. They are, for instance, the veterans' guard at internment camps; I have mentioned 3,000 at Longue Pointe depot working for the British government, and there are the men in the units in the dental and service corps, working for the navy and the air force, and the staffs of the training camps. There are the Army Service Corps personnel, the ordnance personnel, the medical units and all these service units, which are not simply for the purpose of servicing the army of Canada in Canada, but for the purpose of providing a base for equipment and reinforcements for overseas.
Where is the classification with regard to the reserve army for home training, with no intention of going into combat overseas? They are known as the reserve army.
I was going to deal with the reserve army. In reference to the matter of reinforcements-
Before the minister leaves that point, how many of these men are N.R.MA. men?
How are they divided?

Forty-seven per cent of the N.R.M.A. are in operational troops; fifteen per cent are non-operational troops; twenty per cent are in the training stream; eight per cent in the depot reselection and disposal wings and seven per cent are on leave.
What is the total number?
I believe it is 70,000.
Does that include those absent without leave, deserters?
I cannot tell my hon. friend.
We ought to know about that.
I cannot make a complete and comprehensive statement now. Perhaps the hon. member will allow me to continue and he can ask questions afterwards.
You know and we do not. We will ask questions.

I will find out for my hon. friend. With regard to reinforcements, I have a very brief statement which will put the matter clearly. I am glad to be able to say that notwithstanding the fact that a part of the army has been fighting since July, the reinforcement pool overseas is well up to the planned original full strength. This pool was that which was estimated to be adequate to meet battle casualties, and the supply can and will continue to be replenished by the dispatch of further reinforcements from Canada as required. '
There is one qualification to be made. It is very difficult to match supply with requirements of all the different types of tradesmen. Thirty-five per cent of the army to-day are in the different trades, of which there are over 200, many of which are highly specialized. It is a constant battle to get from the population of this country, or for that matter of any country, so large a percentage of skilled men, particularly bearing in mind 'the needs of war industry. The adaptability of young men is such, and the presence of tradesmen throughout the army is so general that I think we can be confident we shall always be able in time of emergency to meet the need.
We have ample trade training facilities and we try well ahead to allocate men during training to meet the requirements which we forecast from the demands that come periodically from overseas. That reinforcement pool overseas will be drawn on as casualties occur; but we estimate that by sending 48,000 men overseas during the fiscal year, 1944-45, we would, on the basis of estimated casualties before us, still end the year with a pool sufficient to maintain the army at the height of its fighting efficiency. To provide that 4,000 a month, we estimate that we shall have
60,000	general service personnel suitable for overseas service in training centres and in units in Canada at the end of March of this year. These, less certain wastage which always occurs from training, will be sent overseas as they complete training or as they are made available by orderly withdrawal from units. That will deplete the number in the training stream. Therefore, to safeguard the future, we are budgeting for an intake of 48,000 general service plus 12,000 N.R.MA.. personnel to release general service personnel, or a total of 60,000 from the total Canadian manpower pool for 1944-45. If we achieved this intake of an average of 4,000 general service men per month it would see us at the end of the fiscal year with reinforcement pool overseas

War Appropriation-Army
maintained at adequate strength, and it would see us with sufficient men in training centres to fight on during 1945.
In the last three months our intake of general service men averaged a little over 3,700. For January it was almost 4,000. What the future will be I do not know, but certainly efforts will be steadily put forth to maintain this January rate. If recruiting should materially fall off it will begin to affect the numbers dispatched overseas in the later months of the fiscal year 1944-45, and should find us at the end of March, 1945, with the pool maintained overseas, but with the number of general service men in Canada reduced approximately by the amount of deficiency in that intake. As a further backlog we have in Canada well over 60,000 N.R.M.A. personnel, of which number perhaps 50,000 could be made available for overseas service if emergency arose and necessary action were taken.
Has there been any increase in that number since last year?

I am sorry I have not the exact figure. I gave the percentages a few minutes ago. In answer to somebody I said
70,000.	I do not think it can be 70,000. I fancy the explanation is that the 70,000 is the number projected as of March 31 while the
60,000	is the number now.
What has been the intake of N.R.M.A. recruits in the same time?
There will be plenty of opportunity to give those figures later and I shall have someone furnish them.
You should have them in the general service statement.

My hon. friend will permit me to make my statement; I cannot have everything at once. I do not think he quite means what he says, when he suggests what I should have and what I should not have. The reinforcement position always depends, of course, on the accuracy of forecast as to casualties and our officers have made a careful study of this factor. I think we have made ample provision in this respect, and therefore, I think I can say to the committee with considerable confidence that our reinforcement position for the fiscal year before us will be well provided for.
Will the minister say that he makes that statement with full confidence?
I cannot say with full confidence; I do not know what the casualties will be.
On the point of reinforcements, will the minister say, in the event of a second front in Europe, on the western front, whether we have adequate reinforcements.
I will say exactly what I have said here.
That does not say anything.
I am saying what anybody would say who had any sense of responsibility.
I have a sense of responsibility, and I resent that.

I have a sense of my responsibility, too; and I say to my hon. friend and to the committee that the casualties have been estimated on the basis of the best information that can be obtained in conjunction with the war office, having regard to the operations which will be carried on, and that is the situation if those casualties are realized. I have said to the committee already that the casualties we have suffered in Italy were somewhat less than those that had been budgeted for.
Are the divisions overseas-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister has expressed the desire to make his statement first, and then he will answer questions.
We are in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are just dealing with the resolution itself; there is no special item before the committee.
Can we not interrogate the minister at all as we go along?

I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver South will recall that last year the practice was to allow the minister to make his statement; then there were at least four or five or six quite lengthy speeches, one of which was made by my hon. friend, before there was any thought of asking questions of anybody or getting down to business. I am glad we are getting down to business earlier this session.
There is another matter to which I wanted to refer; it is just in passing, but at the same time I feel that the armed services should indicate to the committee that they have not lost sight of it. I must say that I have hesitated to talk very much about rehabilitation or demobilization. Sometimes I have been a little concerned at people going overseas to talk to
War Appropriation-Army

our men about rehabilitation and demobilization, knowing as I do and as the country knows what is before us this year.
That the war is not won.

That the war is not won. I felt that it might give the boys an entirely wrong impression, that it might turn their minds from the job they have in hand or perhaps indicate that our minds were being turned from the job which is in hand. At the same time I know enough, from my experience in the Mediterranean area and in England, to realize that naturally the boys are thinking about these things. They are young men who are looking forward to coming back some day, and they want to know what is to be done for them. They do not want charity, but they want to know how they are to be assisted and how they are to be recognized, having regard to the fact that they have been away from employment conditions in this country for a number of years. Of course this is not the particular province of the three armed services; but I wish to say- and in this I am inspired by, and want to give credit to, my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Air-that quite regardless of the fact that pensions and national health, or the veterans' welfare department, or whatever it may be, eventually will take care of the matter, all three services intend to take and are now taking a definite and positive interest in the prospective rehabilitation of soldiers, sailors and airmen. It is not intended that the services should do this by way of providing rehabilitation grants, because those will come after demobilization; it is to be done by looking forward to the time when demobilization may come, endeavouring to plan the relative priorities of the various men who are now in the service, whether it be by length of service, by occupation or what-not. I would not want the committee to take it from anything I say that any policy has been decided upon-but the services want to determine what shall be a fair method of rehabilitation and demobilization; to help the men who remain in the service for a considerable time due to military duties, but duties which may not be as pressing as the duties we see before us this year; to help these men to prepare themselves, looking forward to the time when they will be discharged and return to civilian life.
So each of the three services is setting up a special directorate to deal with demobilization. I do not mean that each directorate is to deal only with the machinery, to decide
fMr. Ralston.]
where the medical examinations shall take place, what forms will be signed, where men should be sent for the purposes of demobilization and discharge, and things of that kind, but it is also to consider and work out what can be done while the men are still in the army, the navy or the air force, to assist in preparing them for their return to civil life. It may be the matter of vocational training, which is being talked about so much; it may be vocational guidance; it may be more education; it may be advice; it may be assistance in some other way to prepare them to return to their rightful place, the place they want in society. These directorates will be headed by men who have had experience in this war, and, I hope, in the last war; men who will understand the problems, the aspirations, the needs and the ambitions of these boys. The directorates will be coordinated by means of an interservice council, so that as nearly as possible we may have the same degree of assistance in the three services by way of vocational training and preparation for civil life, having regard to the facilities provided and the opportunities that present themselves in the service in which the men are engaged now. Further than that, we shall have an interdepartmental council composed of representatives not of the three services alone but of the three services, pensions and national health, labour, and reconstruction, when that department is established. I only mention this to indicate that the services themselves realize their responsibility to those who are still in the service, so that such spare time as these men may have when the active part of the war is over, if they are still retained for military service, shall be utilized in the best possible way, having in mind the desirability of assisting these men in order that they may be prepared to resume the functions of citizens.
Someone asked me about the reserve army. Just a day or two ago a statement was published in this regard, and I should like to give the committee the substance of it. First I want to say that the Canadian army can never acknowledge in too generous terms the work of the reserve army, or the non-permanent active militia as we knew it, and all it has meant in laying the foundation of the Canadian army as it exists to-day. Nearly every unit of our army is founded upon a former militia unit. The names may have been changed, but the personnel, the structure, has remained, and the foundations and traditions are there. If the non-permanent active militia had done nothing more than furnish that

War Appropriation-Army
foundation it would have performed not only a creditable but a vastly important service in connection with the great war of 1939.
That was the original scheme of the non-permanent active militia?
Yes.
They do not always get the credit that is due them, and for that reason I am glad to hear the minister make this statement.

There is no doubt about that. More than that, the non-permanent active militia not only furnished units and helped to mobilize them; it furnished officers as well to take posts not necessarily in their own units but elsewhere, particularly staff -officers in the beginning of the war.
And the people in the non-permanent active militia went to a tremendous amount of trouble and expense.

Not having been a militia man myself, perhaps I can express appreciation more freely than others. I have had occasion to marvel at the time, the energy and the money, as my hon. friend says, that commanding officers particularly, and other officers as well, have put into this work of keeping up the morale of the regiment, making it attractive for men to come in, giving what is perhaps more valuable than money to busy men, namely their time and interest, in order that these young men might have associations with the army, and the benefit of the riper experience of the older ones.

In that case
services have been voluntary.
The service was voluntary, originally, but that could not be expected to continue forever. I think the country was asking too much.
The greatest asset was leadership.

Yes, there is no doubt
about that. We did, as a matter of fact, provide for what we called small administrative and training staffs, for which we paid.

We would have been in
a bad fix when war broke out, if we had not had them.

We would not have had
an organization at all. The reserve army carried on and furnished these units for the active army.
There came a time when I had to come to the house-two years ago I believe it was- and make a statement. I was asked to say
what defence plans we had for Canada, and how we were going to meet the situation on the west and east coasts. I had to speak at that time about the organization of reserve brigade groups, in which reserve units were brigaded for purposes of preparing for actual defence, if defence should be necessary.
At that time, as everybody knows, there was a tremendous upswing in the reserve army, provided by way of additional training equipment, pay and allowances, and by way of extra facilities provided for these units. I think they tided us over, and saw us through at a time which was indeed a very difficult one, before we were able to get going completely with the active army, in full strength.
I believe I have had the opportunity of meeting the officers commanding in almost all districts in. Canada. I have been impressed with the interest, zeal, enthusiasm and selfdenial those men have shown in their desire to help, and in their eagerness to have young men join in order that they might train themselves for whatever task they might have to fulfil in the armed forces.
At that time the reserve army had four roles. One role was a basis of expansion for the active army, in the event of further mobilization. Another was the operational role in the defence of Canada. Another was that of continuing reinforcements to the active army, and the fourth was the duty to aid the civil power.
With that activity there has been strenuous and exacting work done by officers and1 men, including the older men and the boys. Night after night in different armouries they trained in order to see to it that they could do their part, or that they would be ready to do their part in case the need should arise. I know that from different reserve units I have had the request that they might be stationed at some point on the east coast or on the west coast to do their share of duty, as it weTe. Of course that meant a tremendous amount of dislocation in the work of businessmen and others who were members of the reserve units. It would have meant that for the time being the men in those units would have had to sever their connections with the ordinary enterprises in which they were engaged.
Fortunately the situation was such that we did not actually have to use those units for defence. Now, with their background of two years of intensive training and a general increase in efficiency, they are asking, "What will we do now?" It is possible to reassess the demands which we make on the reserve army during this year. It is of course a bulwark against any possible deterioration in the military situation.
War Appropriation-Army

Its role during the coming year is summarized in this way-and I put this first point very high. At the same time it may sound perhaps more psychological than military. The role I mention is that of maintaining throughout the country continued interest in the Canadian Army and its activities, and to set to all citizens an example of preparedness at all times. That is what they have done right through, and I do not think it was needed at any time more than it is now. Many of these men are perhaps working at work benches during the day in munitions factories or in stores or offices or on the farm, but in the evenings they give their time to training, and to fitting themselves for a possible emergency, should the time come. They serve in two ways. I do not know of any better example of "preparedness" than is found in the reserve army.
A second role is that of providing a continuing flow of reinforcements for the forces overseas, by training young men of pre-enlistment age. Another is to back up the civil authority responsible for the enforcement of law and order. Another is that it shall stand as a trained reserve to support the active forces available for the defence of Canada if the military situation should deteriorate, and the last is that it shall be a basis for . expansion of the active' army, should the necessity arise.
The reserve army is insurance against the uncertainties of war. It represents a substantial investment in time, effort and military knowledge on the part of its members. It is sound common sense to maintain that insurance while the risk continues to exist.
While the necessity for the reserve army remains unchanged, it is possible, in view of the improvement in the military situation and the increased efficiency that has been achieved, to decrease the intensity of its training during the coming year. It is therefore proposed: first, to reduce the period of training from forty to thirty days. This will permit a 15-day summer camp, with the remaining fifteen days training carried out at local headquarters, either as forty-five training evenings, or partly evening training and partly week-end exercises.
In addition, provision will continue to be made for the further training of officers, noncommissioned officers and specialists.
Since the reserve army has been operating with a liberal scale of full-time administrative and training staffs for some eighteen months, it is considered that units have now progressed to a stage where their officers and non-com-misioned officers are sufficiently qualified to carry out their training without the same degree of assistance. There will therefore be some reduction in the number employed on full-time training duty.

While no general change in the structure of the reserve army is contemplated, it is proposed that some measure of stream-lining will take place to ensure that all units maintain a satisfactory standard of efficiency. Units unable to maintain a satisfactory strength and efficiency will become dormant for the duration of the war.
In other words, the answer to the reserve army is this: "We want you to carry on, and we believe you are doing a service to Canada in the training which you have undertaken, not only in the record you have made, but because of the interest which you maintain in a community, and through your example of "preparedness." The reserve army assists the young men of sixteen, seventeen or eighteen years who spend their evenings in training with the older men. They are there for the purpose of providing a flow of reinforcements, and that flow has been a most generous one. It will stand back of the civil authority and act with the active force, if necessary. It will be a basis for expansion of the active army, should the necessity arise. We say to them, "You do not need to train quite as intensively as you have done. We have cut the training down by twenty-five per cent from forty to thirty days. We continue to make provision for the training of officers, non-commissioned officers and specialists. We ask you to carry on more of your training yourselves than you have done. And we say, in connection with tnose units which have become more or less dormant, those which are unable to maintain a satisfactory degree of efficiency, 'we will let them lie dormant for the present time'."
Is there a very large percentage which would fall into that class?
I am told there is not.
Why do they become dormant?
I presume it is because of their location, more than anything else. They would be in the more scattered communities.
Might it not be that all eligible men have gone from that district?
Well, as the hon. member knows, the members are men of thirty-five years and over, and boys under age.

Would the
minister give the number in the reserve army?

Although I have not the exact figure, I think it is around 100,000.
It is felt that these changes will give fresh incentive to all ranks of the reserve army to maintain the efficiency that has resulted from the past two years of intensive training. The continued support of employers in encouraging

War Appropriation-Army
their employees to attend annual camps will be of the greatest assistance in carrying out this objective. I wish to say a word of appreciation to employers who have planned so as to allow men to attend these camps.
At great inconvenience to both the men and the employers, sometimes.

A greater measure of responsibility will be placed upon those who have benefited from this training, and the shorter periods of duty will require that all ranks take full advantage of the available training time to maintain the high standard necessary to fulfil the roles allotted to the reserve army. Modem equipment and the latest methods of training will continue to be made available for its use. At the same time appreciable economies will be effected in its cost to the public. Let me emphasize again that the voluntary contribution of time and effort on the part of all ranks in the reserve , army is deeply appreciated and recognized, and it is the purpose of the department to ensure that the demands made upon the reserve army are matched to the changing requirements of the military situation. The standard of training already achieved and the improved strategic situation justify a reduction in the training time required during the coming year, provided full advantage is taken of the reduced period to maintain efficiency.
There is just one last item I wish to put on record before I conclude. I am not going to give any figures now, but I should like to say a word with regard to the Canadian Women's Army Corps. There has been an increase of about 3,000 in the corps this year.
What is the .total now?

I think it is about 14,000. Of the many endeavours which have been put forward to provide agencies to assist in the war none has been more successful, so far as the Canadian army is concerned, than the C.W.A.C. I want to voice the wholehearted and unreserved appreciation of the department for their work and the pride we have in their accomplishments. These young women are serving not only in Canada but in Washington and in the United Kingdom and they would like to serve in other places overseas as well. Where they replace men they are doing their jobs as well as the men, and sometimes better. I think the men will permit me to say that.
There is nothing surprising about that.

They are more nimblefingered and perhaps even more nimble-witted than the men. They have proved a credit to themselves, a credit to the army and a
credit to Canada. I am sure that the committee must take pride in them, seeing them at their work, and on the street. 1 am sure that hon. members would have got a tremendous thrill to have seen the parade I did in London when I attended the service at St. Martin's in the Fields, just before I came back from overseas. They are a great corps and they are doing a magnificent work.
In conclusion, I just want to sound one note of warning. I only wish I could make it. reverberate across this dominion from Sydney to Vancouver. People are being led to believe or they are leading themselves to believe that we have got on so well in winning the war that the collapse of Hitler's Germany is just around the corner. When I was in England there was some talk of the war being over by Christmas; now there is talk of finishing it this year. I hope we do, because every day by which it can be shortened will mean a saving, not just in dollars, but in precious lives and in distress in the homes of Canada and in every other country allied with us.
It is true that we have taken Italy's colonies in North Africa. It is true that we have captured Sicily and about one-third of Italy. It is true that a. small portion of the territory held by the Japanese in the southwest Pacific has been rescued from them. It is a fact that the Russians in their amazing fighting have retaken a lot of the territory which Germany had overrun. But it is also a fact that more than half of the territory taken by the axis forces in their drives of the last three years is still conquered territory. It is a fact that there is not much evidence that German military power has decreased and there is no sign that the Japanese troops have lost any of their willingness to fight and die to hold 'the outposts which protect their home base.
In both Europe and Asia great forces of well-trained enemy troops, well led and well equipped, are ready to fight-and they do fight. Germany dominates Europe. She controls a population of some 325 million. She draws on practically the whole of Europe's industries and economic resources. She has more than 300 well-trained divisions. She has millions of foreign workers in her war industries. It is true that if all the resources of the united nations were pooled we would have an advantage, over Germany in the European theatre. But if it were not for the enormous sacrifices of our Russian ally, who pays the price for magnificent victories, the odds would be roughly four or five to one against us, and these odds would be more unfavourable because of the network of fortifications which the Germans have prepared.
War Appropriation-Army

Let us face the facts. The two major reasons for our optimism for the future-there are others of course-are, first, the ability of our Russian ally to keep nearly three-quarters of the German army occupied in the east and, second, the ability of British, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and United States aviators to keep up their tremendous raids on Germany's European fortress. Germany has shown herself able to stand prodigious losses. At Stalingrad last winter she lost some twenty divisions. Every one of these has been replaced by a new division, well trained and equipped with the latest and best types of weapons. The Germans lost eight divisions in North Africa. Those eight divisions have been replaced with new divisions armed with the most modern equipment. Even last year the Germans reformed, reequipped and raised more than sixty new divisions, each of which had approximately 600 machine-guns and 300 heavier weapons. Included in the armament of these divisions are new models of tanks, self-propelled guns, rocket-guns and other latest type equipment, which in some cases is equal to and in some cases better than anything the allies have.
I am not a pessimist, far from it, but I am a realist. I hope I can make this country realize just what we have ahead of us. It is true that good news has been coming, but remember that if that good news is to continue it can only be by continuous contribution of the matchless price which the men and women of the forces and the homes they come from pay, and only if we are willing to make our contribution in self-discipline and self-denial worthy of theirs.
Let us take a look back and a look ahead. It took three and a half years to clear the enemy out of North Africa. The war has been going on for four and a half years and it is only in the last six months that we have been able to overrun Sicily. The successes we are now having in Italy are just on the fringe of Europe. So far as our land forces there are concerned, we are nearly eight hundred miles from Germany with plenty of formidable opposition and tough ground on our way. The continent of Europe still has to be retaken. The superb fighting in Russia has still to be matched. China must be liberated and Hong Kong avenged. Burma, the Malay peninsula, Singapore and the Philippines must be regained and the southwest Pacific cleared. These enemies of mankind must be forced to unconditional surrender.
Canadians in that tough and heroic fight at Dieppe marked the first turn of the tide toward the land offensive in northwestern
(Mr. Ralston.]
Europe. Canadians in Sicily and Italy helped to mark the first turn of the tide toward the land offensive in southern Europe; Agira and Ortona, to mention only two of many, were epic battles in Canada's war story. But some of the greatest battles of the war are still to be fought, and Canada will be in the thick of it, on sea, on land and in the air.
The message from our troops in Italy and from our troops in England is, "Don't get the idea because good news is coming that the war is about won and that we can slacken a bit." If we were with them in either Italy or England we would not have any delusion that the war is nearly over. We would realize that there is a long way to go yet and that the going will be hard and rough. The way Canadians at home can help to shorten that road is, not by slowing up, but by trying to match the resolution and drive of our soldiers who are fighting Canada's battle in Italy at this very moment and who are at this instant preparing in England for the great offensive.
Their message is, "We are going to stick it; we are going to see it through, but we expect the folks at home to keep up the pressure, not to relax, not to let up." Not long ago we heard the story of the long, grim, stubborn, victorious fight for Ortona. Wounded men refused to be evacuated. Troops asked not to be relieved. They fought on. They won. We at home have to match their fighting spirit with our work, with our determination, with our self-denial, and with our endurance, to back these men of ours to the limit.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked me on Friday, with regard to General McNaughton, at whose instance the medical examinations were made. I told him that I knew the report was transmitted by General McNaughton's direction to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by cable, and that I was not in London at that time, if I remember correctly what I said. I find that the first report, dated November 26, was procured by General McNaughton at his instance and was sent by him to the Prime Minister.
At his instance only?
Yes. I said with regard to the other one that I did not remember just when I received it. I said that I got it-
That is the report of December 11.

Yes-just after I got -back to England on December 10. I find on look-

War Appropriation-Army
ing over my letters that the same day, December 10, I wrote to General McNaughton this letter:
My dear General McNaughton:
As soon as I got in, General Montague-
This is with reference to the first examination?

-gave me your message. As man to man I want to say that I am deeply sorry to find that the situation regarding your health has grown more acute since General Stuart reported to me in Sicily.
That .refers to the first medical report. I received that in Italy.
That is the November 26 one?

Yes. The letter went on:
I do hope and believe that relief from work and rest and change will bring recovery and I shall help all possible to ensure prompt action to facilitate this. I take it that you will be sending me a note so that the matter can be dealt with expeditiously. I understand that apart from Mrs. McNaughton and the doctors, General Montague is the only one who is seeing you but whenever the ban is lifted and you can have it I should be glad to come to visit you at your convenience.
With sincere regret and my remembrances to Mrs. McNaughton and with every good wish to both of you.
Yours very truly,
J. L. Ralston.
What is meant by "when the ban is removed?"
I was told by General Montague that no one was allowed to see General McNaughton on business except the medical men.
How long did that ban extend?
I cannot tell you. I had just got back.
You had seen General McNaughton in November.

Oh, in November?
General McNaughton was not in bed when I saw him at army headquarters. On the 11th of December I got this letter from General McNaughton, dated December 10:
Dear Colonel Ralston:
General Montague has just given me your note of yesterday's date, and I do most sincerely appreciate your kindly consideration of the difficulties in regard to the exercise of the command of the Canadian army in which I am placed by reason of my health. I have spoken to our medical authorities, and it has been
arranged that they will make a further examination this afternoon. I will ask that they furnish you with a copy of their report immediately thereafter; also that the text be cabled to the Prime Minister.
My wife very much appreciates your kind message to her, and she and I will be very happy indeed to see you personally at any time, for I think the doctors are now inclined to let up a bit on the restrictions which they had placed on me.
Very sincerly yours,
A. G. L. McNaughton.
That gives my hon. friend the information with regard to the second medical report which I read to the house the other day.

Were there any other
examinations besides these made of the general's condition, on his own initiative, by civilian doctors or anything of that sort?
I do not know.

Can the minister recall
what was the last date he saw General McNaughton before he went to the North African area?
It was a Sunday. I have this year's calendar in my pocket, not last year's. I think it was Sunday, November the 14th or the 7th; it was a Sunday in any event.

The minister was good
enough to volunteer the information on Friday that when he saw General McNaughton at that time no question of the general's ill health was mentioned1 between the two of them.

Yes; the only thing at
that time was that I recall General McNaughton speaking of the great strain he was under. I think I have mentioned that to the house already. That was the last time I saw him before I went to Italy.
The matter of his health was not an acute subject between you at that time?
I am not going to answer a question of that kind. He spoke of the very great strain which had been on him with regard to some matters-

When did the minister
reach London?
Coming back?

The minister said on
Friday that he met General McNaughton on several occasions before the minister went to North Africa. He has told us that the last time was Sunday the 7th or the 14th.

I have not my diary here.
War Appropriation-Army
Had the minister 'been in London for a week or a fortnight then? He saw the general on several occasions.
I think I had been there altogether about eight or nine days. I saw him soon after I got there.
What the minister says now is that the entire conversation that took place between him and General McNaughton with respect to his health was prior to the minister's having gone to North Africa?

I do not recall now. I
have not attempted to go into detail as to what the general said then. I had a conference with him of an hour or more on that particular Sunday morning. I do not recall speaking of health in the conversations we had prior to that, after I had landed in London and before I went to Africa.
My hon. friend asked another question to which I wish to refer. He said:
My question is whether or not any factors other than that which he mentioned of ill health entered into the resignation of General McNaughton?
I deliberately confined my statement of Friday to the matter of the general's ill health and his own request for his being given leave of absence and relieved of the command) of the army, and I said that I could discuss all other matters connected with the subject but I preferred not to do so because it could do no possible good, particularly at a time like this.
But you did not confine yourself to his ill health, and that is the reason why I asked the question.
I do not know what my hon. friend means.

You did not confine yourself entirely to ill health as the reason for General McNaughton's leave of absence. The minister immediately launched into a question which, I think, raised a doubt in the minds of everyone in the house that ill health was the only factor. The minister spoke about the strong wills of himself and General McNaughton.

Yes. I was dealing with the matter of leave of absence entirely and the contribution that ill health made .to it. I do not follow what my hon. friend means at all. I mentioned, of course, strong wills. I said, "if anybody asked me if we always agreed I would say, 'no'".
I think the general impression was there was some possibility of disagreement. I j.ust want to know whether or not that was a factor.
What is that?

May I explain what I mean? When 'the minister spoke he said he had donfined himself entirely to the matter of ill health. I then rose in my place to explain that he had not confined himself entirely to the matter of ill health but in making his explanation had gone on to refer to the strong wills of himself and General McNaughton. This left the impression, if I may say so, on most members of the house that there was a possibility of disagreement between the government, the minister and General McNaughton. On the basis of that possibility I asked a question as to whether or not there were factors other than ill health which entered into the leave of absence granted to General McNaughton.

I think I can say to my hon. friend that if it had not been for General McNaughton's ill health, leave of absence would not have been granted at the time it was. He would not have been relieved of the command of the Canadian army at the time unless he had requested it. In other words, ill health was the proximate cause.
111 health was 'the proximate cause?
Yes.
The minister has not answered the question.
I am going to deal with that question if my hon. friend will permit me.
I do not want the minister to become angry about it.
I am not angry.
I am trying to get some information. Let us deal with this thing reasonably.

I intimated that there were all sorts of rumours floating about. I said I could go into all of them but that I did not consider it opportune. I preferred not to do it, because it could, to say the least, do no possible good, particularly at times like these. I suggested to the committee, and I suggest to my hon. friend, that when we have a situation which is clearly set forth in the documents which I have read, there can be no question in the mind of anybody that

War Appropriation-Army
leave of absence was necessary and was requested by the general on the ground of ill health. Therefore, is not the supreme question whether General McNaughton was able to carry on at that time, and has anybody any doubt of his inability to do so after reading the documents to which I have referred? I suggest to my hon. friend that makes any other factor simply academic and not applicable to the case. In addition to that practical situation I ask my hon. friend in all sincerity, as I ask myself and the committee, do they think the morale of the Canadian people and the morale of the troops in the field would be promoted by discussions of factors which at the moment and in the circumstances can have no application? Would it not be bound to deserve the rebuke of the men who are in the battle lines at this very instant, or who are preparing to go into battle, if we were to use our time and our energy on a controversy over what might have been, instead of considering how we can train, supply, equip and reinforce these men?
I have already made a statement about our army in Canada and overseas, and the reasons for the dispositions. I ask, is that no more important than the hypothetical question as to whether, although General McNaughton was physically unfit to carry on, there might have been other factors which did not apply? In times like these does the committee think we should spend our time in that way? As I said before, I would prefer not to discuss any other factors. I think the one of health is sufficient. I say to my hon. friend that I am not refusing to do so. I am expressing this view because that is how I feel. I have some personal reasons why it would be far easier for me to go into a discussion of all sorts of things, but I suggest that in the circumstances no good purposes could be served, and I leave it to my hon. friend to decide whether or not he presses that question.

Mr. Chairman, the subject that is before the committee at the moment is the minister's statement with respect to the whole problem of the armed forces. At the last session this subject was proceeded with in a certain very definite way. After the minister had given his statement, item number one on the army war appropriations estimate was called and on that a general. discussion took place. I take it that the government is prepared at this time to follow the same procedure.
This afternoon I wish to avail .myself of the privilege that has been accorded in the past and follow the same procedure. I refer the 100-29
minister to certain questions which I asked on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Some of those questions have not been answered. Some of them have been answered to the satisfaction of the minister, but not entirely to the satisfaction, if I may say so, of the committee as a whole. One of the questions asked at that time will be found at page 19 of Hansard of January 31, and is as follows: "What is being done with our big home defence army?" As the minister has indicated, that is an army comprising some
70,000	people. The minister now shakes his head. The figures I jotted down are, "70,000 in the home defence army."

No. If my hon. friend will permit me, the operational troops number something like 55,000. These people are distributed, as I indicated, in the home defence army. They are distributed on different jobs. The home defence army, so called, or the operational troops in Canada number about
55,000.	I think I said forty-seven per cent of the N.R.M.A. were in these units.

I think that pretty well illustrates another point which I intend to bring up, namely, that in the discussion which occurs from time to time in connection with the armed forces, the average layman is confused by the conflict of terms of a military nature which he does not always understand.
You invented that term; I did not.

Perhaps I did. I may invent some more during the discussion which I hope will be applicable to the situation. What the public wants to know is how many men are in uniform in Canada who are not available for overseas service or, in other words, fall into the category of those called under the National Resources Mobilization Act who have not volunteered for service outside Canada. My understanding is that that number is something like 70,000 men. If that is so, I should like the minister to take note of these supplementary questions. I should like him to answer the question I asked on January 31, which was, has the government given consideration to whether or not these men are going overseas or whether or not the personnel is to be directed back to civilian activities in Canada, or what actually is to be the final disposition of those 70,000 men? I think the minister ought to give us all the information in regard to the cost of these 70,000. I should like to know the yearly cost of maintaining that army of 70,000, because the question becomes very important from another angle.

War Appropriation-Army

Since Kiska the whole question of the army of
70.000	has been altered to some extent. In addition to that, the government has seen fit pretty well to withdraw and to abandon in many sections the whole A.R.P. activity, which would indicate clearly that the government is of the opinion that the whole question of the invasion of Canada and, in consequence, the whole question of the defence of Canada has undergone a major change. I wish the minister would give these figures when he speaks again in the debate.
The minister has referred to General Mc-Naughton. I approach the whole question with regard to General McNaughton with as serious a sense of responsibility as anyone in public life could have. I agree with the minister that the name of a great Canadian, the name of one who has achieved great things with Canada's army, should not unnecessarily form the subject of a mere political discussion in this parliament during the war.
I think all members of the committee will feel as I do this afternoon when I say that personally I have not made a sufficient contribution in the war to be able to say very much about' those in our armed services who have done so much more. In the early stages of the war many of us did apply for enlistment in the armed services, and some of us have tried, as far as it lay in our power to do so, to serve our countiy; but I am frank to say that I have always felt that my contribution is rather puny, measured by any yardstick, when contrasted with what has been done by those who are in far more dangerous fields of activity than we are.
From that point of view, I am very conscious of the whole situation with regard to General McNaughton. I think we ought to look at the government's problem, and the problem of those men and women who are in the armed services overseas and in Canada, with a mind bent upon doing the best we can for them and for the country at this time. Whatever may be the responsibility -and the minister assesses some responsibility to the opposition in this regard-I would point out to him that it was not the opposition or members of this house who created the situation upon which the public has been demanding so much enlightenment, particularly in the past few days. I would have felt a rather heavy responsibility if that situation had been created by us; nevertheless, as the Prime Minister very properly pointed out a few days ago, the opposition in parliament has an obligation to the people. Therefore, subject to security reasons and the whole question of the national interest, and subject further, if I may say so, to the desire that the names of

those men who have done so much to preserve and maintain this country during this time of war, and who are in our armed services, should not be made a matter of mere political discussion, it seems that the minister also has a heavy responsibility in denying to the country at this time as much information as he is actually withholding at this moment.
I have not denied it.

I asked the minister at the end of the sitting on Friday a question which was not designed to throw this problem into the arena of parliament; rather, I was hoping that he would then, by a simple answer, be able to clear up the whole situation. I tried to interrupt him on one occasion in order that he might have that opportunity in an early part of the debate, and I put the question again at the end, so that he would have notice of it for to-day. The question was a very simple one which the minister could have answered readily, but he has not answered it this afternoon. The question is this: Were there other factors, other than ill health, which entered into the whole problem of the resignation or leave of absence of General McNaughton?

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had not quite concluded the observations I intended to make in connection with this part of the discussion on the war appropriation measure. I should like in my remarks this evening to refer to one or two matters mentioned by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) on Friday and again this afternoon.
I refer first to a matter which perhaps some who are not too familiar with the situation might regard as of minor importance, compared with other matters which were the subject of discussion. Nevertheless it seems to me that the matter to which I am about to refer is one of great significance and one which has assumed great importance. The fact that the Minister of National Defence returning from theatres of war overseas saw fit to use the House of Commons as a venue for the giving of information, to give a lead to the people of Canada, indicates the importance of the matter to which I now refer, namely, the delivery of mail to our men and women in the armed services.
I regard with some pride the fact that I have a heavy overseas correspondence. My
100-29J
experience indicates there is scarcely anything more valuable to our overseas troops than the maintenance of a regular mail service. Whatever we in parliament can do to arouse the people of our country to a point where they will keep closely in contact with those who have left our midst might be regarded as a signal service to Canada, and to those who serve overseas.
I am not sure whether it was the Minister of National Defence or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who said that in some instances men have spent their fifth Christmas away from home. I believe it was the Prime Minister who said that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Just think of that! The fact of the matter is that because of the trend of the war our troops have been left for a long period of time without action. That fact has, in my view, made it even more essential for our people to assume the responsibility of seeing to it that our men and women in the armed forces are not disregarded, so far as keeping in close touch with them is concerned.
I said something this afternoon about the contrast between the contribution made by those of us in civilian life and that made by the forces in the armed services. Sometimes we are apt to put too much stress on what is done on the home front. The home front is important; and those connected with it have done a great job. But let us not in the same breath mention the service, the contribution and the sacrifice of those who are on active fronts, protecting us in the theatre of war. That being so, surely those of us in the civilian population can make sure that those boys and girls who have gone from our midst are assured, by communications from time to. time, that they are still part and parcel of the Canadian people. I make these observations to-night to emphasize a matter which, to my mind, is of greater importance than it may appear to be at first glance.
I was pleased, too, to hear the minister make reference to the work of the Canadian Women's Army Corps, and I join with him, in paying a well-deserved tribute to that branch of the service. I would couple with that observation a similar expression with respect to the women in the other two branches, namely the air force and the navy. No reflection is intended upon other branches of the service when I mention these three services specially. The reputation the womenfolk in the armed services have gained, and
War Appropriation-Army

the splendid work they have performed should not go unnoticed by a grateful country and parliament.
Then the minister touched upon, but did not discuss at length, the rehabilitation of the men and women in the services. I would agree with the minister, and I believe most people would agree with him when he says that the main emphasis must be placed upon matters more urgent and more acute than those connected with demobilization. I agree with him when he says that the winning of the war must come before demobilization. The seriousness of the job was impressed upon us this afternoon, when the minister pointed out that the war has not yet been won, and that we may be some considerable distance from that result. So that the whole problem of rehabilitation and demobilization must come in its turn.
However, while that may be, the government must be prepared for the possibility of a speedy ending, and it must not be caught unprepared for the peace. The fact that we were not prepared for the eventualities of war cost us a great deal in life, limb, property and finance. Let us make sure that when peace comes upon us we shall not be unprepared.
This brings up the whole question of the rehabilitation of our men. and women in the services. While I take my position with the minister in his statement as to the relative importance of rehabilitation compared with the immediate problems of the war, nevertheless I think he will agree when I say that we must not disregard the problems connected with demobilization. This has been the subject of many conversations. Much has been said about what is to be done for the man who comes back from the war by way of placing him in a peace-time pursuit.
I pass on to the minister-and also to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), who might lend an ear to this-what has been told to me by men who have returned from overseas. It is all very well to speak about putting our soldiers, sailors and airmen on the land. In itself, however, that is not sufficient. It is all very well to talk about giving them education. But again, that in itself is not enough. Our men and: women who will return must not be placed in a position where they will feel that those civilians who have been able to save victory bonds, war savings certificates and the like are placed in a better position, in respect of ready cash and security, than those who have done the fighting. The whole problem of gratuities, the whole problem of providing

for the men and women of our armed forces something in the nature of ready cash, if you want to put it that way, when they come back and when they take up their jobs must be considered so that they will not be penalized in favour of those who stay at home for various reasons or were unfit to go, but shall be placed, not only on an equal footing with our civilians but, if I may say so, on a preferred footing. That must be the position of the men and women of our armed forces in any demobilization and rehabilitation scheme. I want to caution the government to see that these plans have been completely worked out by the time they are to be put into use.
I have no intention to-night of taking up any undue time of the committee because when the resolution was originally moved into committee I indicated that it was the intention of our party to make a close scrutiny, investigation and audit of the expenditures of the government when we were in committee. I have simply outlined one or two points which I thought were of salient interest and importance to the public and to parliament. I hope that as the discussion progresses we shall be furnished with as full and complete answers to the questions that have been asked as is possible to give in order that we may have the information to which the public is entitled.

I do not propose to
speak at any length to-night because last Friday I expressed the opinion that we should be discussing the details of these estimates when the bill was before us. I still feel that the time spent in two debates, one on the resolution and one on the bill, is time that is-I shall not say wasted, but duplicated. I should like to see the house proceed with the bill.
However, there is one thing I wish to say to the Prime Minister. Just before we rose for dinner to-night he suggested that in view of the interest shown in and the questions asked about the retirement of Lieutenant-General McNaughton he would be very glad to have the leader of the opposition, the leader of the Social Credit group and myself meet him in the near future, to-morrow morning I believe, for the purpose of seeing the correspondence.
I am glad to accept that invitation, but I have a suggestion to make. It is that we Should have this . meeting and invite Lieutenant-General McNaughton to be present.
