Very often official documents and correspondence, because of their nature, need to be supplemented by personal explanations. I think in viewing this correspondence we could gauge the situation much more intelligently if Lieutenant-General McNaughton were present.

War Appropriation-Army
I do not know whether it would be possible to have him present to-morrow morning, but I think t'he meeting should be held at once and I am using the term "at once" to mean as soon as possible. In the interests of the government andl of those who have to read this correspondence and come to some decision in order that they may advise their colleagues I urge the Prime Minister to take steps to see that. Lieutenant-General McNaughton is present when this correspondence is examined.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the
first meeting should be between the leaders of the different parties of this house and myself. When we come together and discuss the matter we can then consider the point raised by my hon. friend.

I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question since I was not present just before the dinner recess. If there is any correspondence in existence which has not yet been revealed and made public and which it is now proposed to make public to the leaders of the respective parties and I believe to my colleague, the hon. member for Yale, should that correspondence be kept private or are these gentlemen to be at liberty to divulge to their followers the contents of the correspondence? If that be so, is there any good reason why the correspondence should not be tabled? Why the secrecy about the matter? If the Prime Minister will say on his responsibility, not that it is not in the public interest, because that is the stock phrase, but that for reasons of security, having regard to the times in which we are living or for some other reason similar to that, it should not be made public, then I shall be content.
I know nothing about the matter, but the public mind has been raised to the point where they desire to know more about it. If the truth bears heavily upon someone, and I do not know whom, then the truth will not hurt anyone. I invite the Prime Minister to take us into his confidence. If he will say that because of national security or for some other good reason it is not wise that this correspondence should be made public, then I shall not question his decision. I do not rise in my place to make an issue because I do not know anything about this matter.
I have a sincere * regard for General McNaughton. I was associated with him for a brief period some years ago. I thought then he was a man's man, and I still think so. The government selected him to lead the Canadian troops overseas in November, 1939, and the whole country applauded that action and supported the government in its selection.
May I pause here to express my personal sympathy with General McNaughton if after four years or more of very strenuous life he finds himself in perhaps not as healthy a condition as he ought to be. I think every one of us will be sympathetic, but I am inquiring now if there is any good reason why the public should not know the truth about this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
First of all, may I answer my hon. friend's question with regard to security. I am glad that he has raised the point. As he will be the first to know, telegrams come in cipher code and I have to consider the responsibility, and the government has to consider the responsibility of making public, telegrams or correspondence in the terms in which they come to the government and thus divulge what may lead to the government's code being deciphered and use being made of it by the enemy. That of itself is a clear reason why correspondence which has come in cipher code and which has been deciphered should not be made public, certainly not in the exact terms in which it appears. That "le real embarrassment and handicap the government is under in this matter. It has no desire to keep secret information the public ought to have, but it does desire to safeguard in every possible way great public considerations of which full account has to be taken. There is the further fact to be considered. Whatever is disclosed in connection with this subject cannot be other than of great concern, not only to the people of Canada but to the government of the United Kingdom, the government of the United States, and indeed to the governments of all the united nations. I am perfectly sure that when the hon. leaders of the different parties learn at first hand of the matters on which they wish to be informed, they will find little difficulty in agreeing with the government as to the best course which should then be pursued.
As to placing any obligation on the leaders of the parties who may see the correspondence or be advised of it, I need not say that all three leaders are honourable gentlemen and I place no restrictions on them whatsoever as to what they may wish to say or do as to informing or advising the members of their respective parties. I do not wish to impose any restrictions upon them, beyond those imposed upon each by his own conscience.
The government's action in this matter, as I have already said, is entirely begotten of a desire to protect the war effort not only of this country but of the united nations to the fullest extent possible and to protect all parties concerned therewith.
War Appropriation-Army

May I say to my hon. friend who has spoken of his admiration for Lieutenant-General McNaughton that I am one of those who had to do with the appointment of General McNaughton, and I have always held him in the highest possible esteem. I would be the last'to wish to have any step of mine in any way embarrass General McNaughton or deprive him of any privilege that he may wish .to have. I cannot, however, see that in taking the course which I am now suggesting of having the leaders of the different parties come together and consider all that may be before them, I shall be taking any step that will be prejudicial to anyone, let alone to General McNaughton.
, Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): Mr. Chairman, one word more. I had intended to make reference to. the proposal of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that General McNaughton should be invited to meet this committee. May I say that, at first blush at all events, T deprecate that suggestion for 'this reason: it would simply be an invitation to crossexamine General McNaughton. I do not think the stage has been set for .that or anything like that, and I hope that will not happen.

The purpose of my suggestion was not to cross-examine General McNaughton but rather because I know from experience extending over some years that public documents do not always contain all that there is to know, and to complete the picture one sometimes needs public documents to be supplemented by those who are involved in matters which public documents discuss. I think every member of this House of Commons knows the nature of official documents. Otherwise it seems to me that what we would be actually doing would be hearing one side of the story if we merely see the correspondence, and I do not think it is quite fair-if I may put it this way- 'to leave the party leaders to make a decision as to whether their colleagues in the house should be advised of all the circumstances or not. I do not think that is placing us in a proper position with regard to our colleagues or with regard to the house and the country. That is what I had in mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that he will be at the meeting in the morning and I shall be very happy if he will see that his interest is protected in every particular.
In order that there may be no misunderstanding as to my attitude toward General McNaughton at this time or in regard to the
LMr. Mackenzie King.]
matters we are discussing, may I give to the committee immediately the telegram I sent to General McNaughton at the time he relinquished the command of the Canadian army. This was not in code. It was sent to the high commissioner to transmit to General McNaughton.
Would the Prime Minister give the date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is dated Ottawa, December 26, 1943, and reads:
Dear General McNaughton:
As you relinquish your command of the Canadian army I desire, on behalf of the government and people of Canada, to thank you for the great service you have rendered. our country and other of the united nations from the beginning of the war. I sincerely trust that, freed from the very heavy responsibilities which have been yours over the past four years, your health and strength may speedily be restored.
The word that you have had to relinquish command of the army will be received throughout Canada with feelings of deepest regret. May it not be long before our country may again have the full benefit of your wide experience and exceptional abilities.
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister.

Perhaps I misunderstood the admonition of the Prime Minister at six o'clock, but as I understand him, his desire was that this whole question of General McNaughton and his resignation should be a closed book until such time as the leaders of the different parties had an opportunity to discuss it. But now, first of all, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar interjects with new suggestions, and then the Prime Minister comes along and reads a telegram. If we are to heed the Prime Minister's admonition I think we had better end further debate on this matter at this time. I am quite surprised that the Prime Minister should have introduced that telegram; and if this keeps up I do not know where we are going to end. I have been trying to carry out the Prime Minister's wishes because I thought it was in the national interest not to prolong this debate now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend heard what his colleague the hon. member for York-Sunburj'' suggested, he would see it was a statement that seemed to me to necessitate or render advisable by giving to the committee the telegram I had sent in the open to General McNaughton at the time.

It did not strike me in that way.

War Appropriation-Army

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope there is nothing in the message which anyone in the nouse will take exception to one way or the other at this time. I am only too ready to say nothing further about this matter at all until hon. gentlemen opposite have made their wishes known.

It seems to me without doubt advisable that nothing more be said at this stage on this matter until the meeting takes place, and I thank the right hon. gentleman for his courtesy in asking me to join with the three leaders. He does so, I know, because for a year or so I occupied the position of Minister of National Defence, and during that time Lieutenant-General McNaughton was Chief of the General Staff. I never can forget the admiration in which I held General McNaughton, the assistance that he was, the ability that he showed and the experience which he had, and it is a matter of no little sorrow to me that General McNaughton's health at the moment is not such as to enable him to carry on the arduous duties for which he was responsible.	*
I cannot find myself in agreement with the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, reiterated again to-day, that we should do well to cut short all debate in the committee stage on this resolution and that the debate should take place on the bill. I think he was in error the last time he referred to it when he stated that the bill would have the schedules attached and that they would come before the Chair item by item. That is not the case. War appropriation bills of recent years have had no schedules attached. I have always understood that one of the reasons for making it a different bill from the ordinary money bill was that the government sees fit-perhaps quite rightly so-to keep a certain amount of flexibility within its grasp with regard to these expenditures. The fact remains that on a bill such as this there is no schedule attached, and it appears to me that it does not make very much difference from the point of view of saving time or wasting it whether the discussion takes place at this stage or at that. There is a reason why I prefer that it should take place at this stage. In matters as complicated as this one, subjects frequently arise which have to do with not one minister or two but perhaps three; and when such matter is discussed we may, after hearing the first minister and his views thereon, have an opportunity of hearing a second minister, and it may cover the doings of three departments. It may very well be that after the discussion has taken place questions arise on which clarification is required. When the bill comes up
in the committee stage for second reading we have an additional opportunity to obtain more information if we so desire. To my mind that is the reason why it is well to have the discussion take place at this stage; and we are able to go back again to the bill if it is necessary. Last year it was not necessary. Hon. members will remember that the war appropriation bill was completed only two days before prorogation, and appears in a short paragraph in Hansard. The introduction of the bill, first reading, second reading, committee stage and third reading all took place in that short space of time. No advantage was taken of the opportunity to discuss the bill at that time. But if I remember rightly, in the year before when the war appropriation bill was brought down such discussion was of great value when the bill came up the second time. Therefore I prefer the method which we have found our way into in this war for dealing with discussion on these estimates. The government shows it is fully inclined to give us all the information in detail. The first sheet is before us. We can open it up for discussion, and I have no doubt there will be no impediment placed in our way in our endeavour to obtain the information we require.
There is a matter that I want the Minister of National Defence to refer to again in clearer terms than he did, because I am in just as much of a fog as I ever was with regard to this army in Canada, which some people call a home army and some call the defence army. I remember the minister said last session that there was no such thing as a defence army. I do not know what it is called to-day, but the description which the minister gave this afternoon has left me as much befogged as I ever was, and lest it be thought it is merely my dullness of mind, may I say that I find a considerable number of my fellow members are also quite befogged as to what this army consists of and what it is doing.
It is not easy, without Hansard of this afternoon before us, to follow the minister's description. The picture that I have is that in Canada there is a training stream which amounts to 70,000 men and which is looked upon in the main as the reinforcements which in due course will find their way overseas. These reinforcements, plus such reinforcements as exist in the holding units overseas are, in the minister's opinion, sufficient to meet the estimate of casualties for five divisions [DOT] overseas at the present time. At the other end of the scale, if I may so describe it, we find the reserve army. The reserve army consists of the units that were known as the non-permanent active militia. I am very glad
War Appropriation-Army

the minister took the opportunity to pay tribute to the officers and men of the nonpermanent active militia. It was set up twenty or more years ago. It was a skeleton force in my day and amounted to 55,000 men. It was to be the nucleus capable of being expanded into the necessary armed forces when war came. These officers and men stayed loyally with the reserve army, doing the drudgery through the years of depression and years of peace. I do not think too high praise can be given them. I have known them in the units in my particular neighbourhood. I have known them in other units, and I have always felt great appreciation for what these men gave up to keep their unit of the reserve army in something like its proper shape. The minister did not praise them any too highly and I know his words will be appreciated by many who have come in contact with them. That reserve army, he tells us, amounts to about 100,000; and it is in between these two extremes of the military forces that I want clarification.
Excluding the reserve forces, I understand that the remainder of the soldiery here or overseas, compose the active army. Certain of them, for reasons well known, will not under present regulations leave this country. They will be used in defence. Did I understand him to say that in the active army in Canada there were 55,000 operational troops and 75,000 troops rendering service to the operational troops and that it covered the veterans' guard, training establishments and the great number of incidental units? "What I do not understand is, will those 55,000 men be available for the training stream if and when need arises? That is one of my difficulties.
Another of my difficulties is to follow him in his description of how the national resources mobilization men compose forty-seven per cent of the operational troops here, and if that is so how can they be considered a part of that stream which may eventually be trained for overseas? To my mind there is considerable confusion with regard to those who are not reserve, those who are not in the training stream, those who are at the present time in Canada preparatory to defence, shall I say? Included in that is the contingent that went to Kiska and came back. What is happening to them? Are those units being broken up now that they are being distributed through the Canadian active army in Canada, or are they finding their way into the training stream?
It is commonly said that in a good many parts of Canada-I shall mention Petawawa for one-there are a very large number of men with their complement of officers, with

their necessary supporting supply forces, and there are unattached officers by the dozen. I do not know if that is an accurate statement, but the minister will be able to inform us. It is commonly believed that, scattered across Canada, there are a very considerable number of officers who do not appear to be attached to any unit at the moment and who are marking time or doing something or another or doing nothing at all. It is all these matters which I think the minister will do well to explain to us and through us to the people of Canada. *

First, with regard to troops in Canada, I find it a little difficult to follow my hon. friend. He speaks of the number of N.R.M.A. personnel in Canada and talks about the home defence army. I have endeavoured to make it clear that there is no such thing as a home defence army. There is a Canadian active army, and in units of that army, in detachments of it, there are men who are N.R.M.A. personnel who at the present time are not liable without further action to service overseas. But they are serving in the Canadian active army; they are not hived or segregated. They are filling a place which is necessary at the present time in Canada, doing a job that somebody else would have to do if they were not there. That applies in connection with operational troops of whom 34,950 are N.R.M.A. personnel.
That is, of the 55,000?
Yes. In the non-operational troops the proportion is very much lower, about 11,000, and in the training stream there are 15,000 out of approximately 75,000.

Have they volunteered for
overseas?
No.
Then how can they be in the training stream heading for overseas?

The training stream is heading both for overseas and for service in Canada. When you call a man up you have to train him whether he is to serve in Canada or overseas. In the depot, reselection and disposal units there are 6,400, and on extended leave, about 5.300. So that these men are scattered all through the services in Canada, and it is quite true that they are not available for overseas service until further action is taken. But there seems to be an idea that these men are sitting down doing nothing because they are not for overseas service at the present time. If you did not have them, however, you would have to have some other men in their place.

War Appropriation-Army
Why does the minister say that? There is no danger of invasion.
I have heard that so often.
It will bear repetition.

I heard it from this part of the house when I was minister in 1926-30; "What are you preparing for? There is no war." I maintain that we do not have these operational troops just for fun. They are on the east coast and on the west coast, in coast defence batteries, in close support battalions, searchlight companies and in all the posts which are necessary for the purpose of taking care of the scale of attack which has been agreed to, not simply by our own chiefs of staff but by the United States chiefs of staff as well, and the 55,000 form a comparatively small number. That is what these troops are for.
The hon. member for Yale asks with regard to troops going overseas, and reinforcements. He wants to know what the situation is. I said that the reinforcement pool overseas is well up to the planned strength; that is to say, it is a pool over there to be drawn on as casualties occur, and as that pool goes down it is refilled by men sent from here. If the casualties are heavy at a particular time the pool will go down considerably, but the general dispatch is more or less in regular monthly shipments, with the result that at the end of the year you will have averaged up and the pool will be back to what it was at the beginning, provided the casualties have not exceeded the rate at which the reinforcement pool was at first built up.
And that pool overseas amounts to the estimate of the casualties that may be anticipated for the five divisions overseas?

For a certain period, based on a certain number of months intense activity and a certain number of months of operations of varying degrees of intensity, as is figured out, having regard to the operations which are visualized.
There has been some statement about divisions sent to Italy in order to avoid or to lessen the necessity for reinforcements. There has not been a single change of any kind in the scales of casualties for which we have estimated, owing to the fact that we sent divisions to the Mediterranean-no change whatever.
I never heard that, but you have reinforcements there, I hope.

It has been said. The suggestion was that the corps was sent to Italy because the government had not reinforcements sufficient to keep them up at the rate which was estimated, taking cross-channel operations into account. The estimate of casualties has been based on the iftost careful computation possible in view of the experience our men have had, and the figures I gave out this afternoon are figures in which my officers believe. They have been overseas themselves consulting with the authorities, and they anticipate that if these estimates are based on sound grounds, which they have every reason to believe is tire case, the reinforcement situation will be as I have stated.
The minister did not give the figures on reinforcements.
Yes; my hon. friend did not hear me. -
What is considered an adequate reinforcement pool in percentage in relation to the active army overseas?

Of course I cannot give that information. I have been asked for it before. It is regarded as one of the most secret pieces of information from the point of view of security, but I assure my hon. friend that it is based not simply on a Canadian estimate but on a British estimate as well.
What is the estimate based on-on the history of casualties in this wTar? If that is so, it is very small for Canada.

I can only say to my hon. friend that it is based on what competent officers think is a scale which is not likely to be exceeded in connection with the sort of operations they visualize, and that applies not simply to the Canadians but to the British as well. I have already explained that that reinforcement pool is there, and as it is lowered by casualties it is filled by troops sent over. These troops are in the training stream at. the present time, being trained, they are also in operational units. We are withdrawing these men from operational units from time to time, retraining them when necessary, and sending them overseas, replacing them with N.R.M.A. personnel. That in short is the situation. I was frank with the committee and pointed out that if recruiting went down perceptibly, if it did not keep up, it would

War Appropriation-Army

mean that at the end of the fiscal year, 1944-45, 'towards the end, the pool in Canada would drop, although the pool overseas would [DOT]have been kept up.

Has not that contingency arisen now-that recruiting has dropped and dropped materially, and that an effort is being made now, through the draft boards, according to recent instructions, to increase the number of men to be taken in?

I do not know what my
hon. friend is referring to. All I have to say is that I believe the number being requested from the draft board has remained constant for the last six months, at least, and I am sure there has been no effort as far as the Department of National Defence is concerned' to have any increased number called.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before we proceed further I would suggest, not for my own sake but for the sake of preserving order, that hon. members address their remarks to the chair.

I have a suggestion to
make, if it is agreeable to the committee. We have 'here the statement and the various headings under which these expenditures are being considered by the committee. Would it not help us all; would it not enable us to formulate our questions better and perhaps let us make better preparation to answer them, if we did as we do with ordinary estimates, that is, proceed with the items as they are set out here, in the order in which they appear? I may say to anyone who is interested in the mobilization act, for instance, that this matter can be taken up very easily under pay and allowances, which includes national resources mobilization personnel. The first item on the list is civil salaries and wages. I am' in the hands of the committee, but I think this procedure is generally understood to be the best to follow, and perhaps we might make better progress; I might be more informative, and perhaps be a little more ready to answer, if we proceeded in that way.

While we are discussing this question of organization and this reinforcement pool, I should like to ask the minister whether these divisions

I think he referred to three in Britain and, I suppose, the two that are in Italy-are up to war strength now'. Are all these divisions fully manned and up to war strength at the present time?
Yes.

From what the minister said I gathered that the training stream, or whatever term he applied, included' the men (Mr. Ralston.]
who are in the defence army of Canada, so called by the public, the men staying in Canada-

My hon. friend is starting his question with an assumption which is not correct. I understood- him to say that he gathered that the training stream consisted of the defence army in Canada. The training stream consists of all the men who are in training either for overseas or for Canadian service.
I think in the minister's statement he said that training stream numbered about 50,000; I believe that was the figure used.
It is about 75,000 altogether. [DOT]

That included others as well, but we will use the figures, fifty to seventy-five thousand. Does the minister feel that this is the number that will be maintained as a training stream or whatever he wishes to call it? Does he feel that this will be the approximate number that will be held here in Canada?

No. As I was saying, the training stream is drawn upon from time to time as dispatches are made overseas; and as recruiting is carried on the training stream is refilled. I said that if recruiting went dowm in July or August, for instance, it would mean, that the output of the training stream perhaps next January or February would be lower, due to the fact that fewer men had gone in.

The minister misunderstood me. Do I understand, then, that in practice, according to the minister's ideas, that number of fifty to seventy-five thousand must be maintained in order to carry out the policy which has been adopted bs- the department; in other words, that this many men will still remain inactive in Canada, in a sense, possibly in preparation for going overseas if they ever go overseas? It keeps fifty to seventy-five thousand men static in Canada; that is what I mean.
They are not static.
Well, that is what it amounts to.
They are not static; they are being trained.

Trained for what
purpose?
Trained for overseas.

But fifty thousand or more of them are not going overseas?

War Appropriation-Army

I interrupted my hon. friend to tell him that I thought he was labouring under a misapprehension. In the training stream at the training centres there are about fifteen thousand who are National Resources Mobilization Act personnel. At the present time these men are not going overseas, but they are being trained for the purpose of taking the place of general service personnel in units, to release those men so that they may go overseas. But those units have to be kept up. I have explained some of the functions of the operational units, and I have gone into the functions of the non-operational units as well. These units have to be kept up in order to supply the ordnance and so on, and to supply the personnel to do all the work of a base for the provision of our army overseas.
Then are we to have only fifteen thousand men in Canada who are not going overseas?
No. We have 15,000 in the training centres; we have 34,000 in the operational units, and we have 11.000 in the non-operational units.
That is 50,000 or more.

Altogether it comes to over
70.000	men. Included in that number are 5.300 who are on extended leave, that is to say farm leave, mining leave, forestry leave and so on. They are all included in that number.

Will the minister give the committee a statement of the number of men in Canada, in all capacities, drawn to the colours under the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act, at present in the training stream or in units, operational or otherwise? How many of these draftees have we on the payroll in Canada to-day, where are they and what are they doing?

This is the third time I have given that information, but I will give it half a dozen times if the committee wants it. In operational troops, that is in units, there are roughly 34,000. In non-operational troops there are roughly 11,000.

What are the duties of those
11.000	men?
What is that?

My hon. friend asked for the information; surely he will give me an opportunity to furnish it. These men are in ordnance depots. I think of the central mechanization depot at London; I think of the Longue Point depot; I think of the training centre at Barriefield; I think of hospitals all over the country; I think of district headquarters; I think of camp staffs; I think of army service corps. All these men are nonoperational troops. In the training stream there are 15,000 being trained.

That is
60.000.
Then in the depot, the rc-selection wing I spoke of, where they arc being moved from one place to another, posted to a new place and so on, there are 6,400; and on extended leave there are 5,300.
That is approximately 70,000, all told.
And as I pointed out to the committee, if they were not there somebody else would have to be there, drawing the same money.
We heard all that. These 70,000 men are all in good military categories, capable of fighting?
No, they are not.

What
categories are 'they in, then?
They are category "A", category "B", and some as low as category "C".
How many in categoiy "A"?
I could not tell my hon. friend; I could only make a rough estimation.
Perhaps my hon. friend can give that later on.
At a rough guess I would say probably 50,000.

I may as well tell the minister now that the public want 'to know how many men there are among these zombies, as they are commonly called, who are in category "A", the highest category, and who are not fighting, who are not intended to fight and who do not. intend to fight.
War Appropriation-Army
Like the Kiska troops, for example?
I expect they are part of it.
They were part of it. They seemed 'to have some intention of fighting.

In the break-down the minis-fter has given he has placed the number of recruits called under the National Resources Mobilization Act at around 70,000. I should like to draw his attention to the table which .appears in the January, 1944, issue of Canada at War, at page 22. It shows the total number called as 125,640, from which number there is subtracted the number of men who transferred to the other various forces, numbering 37,930. That leaves a remainder of 87,710, as of September 30, 1943. Since that time no doubt many thousands of others have been, called, which brings the number up to -around 100,000. Would the minister explain where these 30,000 men are, between the
70,000	he has given, and the total to date of 100,000.

I think my hon. friend has the explanation right in that book. I think the footnote in the book will tell him that. 1 have not the book in front of me, but I think it is the case that the figures he has given are intake, and they have made no allowance for discharges. The difference lies in those who have been discharged. I think if my hon. friend would read the note he would see if it is not what I say it is.
Which note?
I have not the book here. Is not the first note one which says that-certain figures are not included?

It says:
Figures of intake do not represent actual strength of the armed services, as they do not take into consideration men discharged for medical or other reasons.
I am talking about actual strength. My hon. friend is talking about gross intake.

But I would point out to the minister that if these men are called up and enrolled under the National Resources Mobilization Act, it is doubtful that there would be any number up in the thousands discharged.

I am sorry if my hon. friend is doubtful, but I am giving him what the strength is. And there are discharges. I think if my hon. friend has the figures he will see these enrolments began in 1941.
fMr. R. B. Hanson.]
It is up to September 30, 1943.
Those are enrolments since the beginning of the war?
Yes.

And there have been those
discharges.
Well, then, would the minister be good enough to complete this statement, and show us the number of discharges?

I cannot give it in that way. The only way to do is to give my hon. friend the strength. I have given that to him. My hon. friend is doing what others are doing who take the total enrolments in the last war and treat that as the strength of the army.
The last war?

Yes, the last war. They are comparing this war and the last war, and saying there were 619,000 in the last war, when it was 619,000 men enlisted and conscripted. It was not 619,000 on the strength of the army.
Is it correct to say that of these 125,000 called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act there have been some 30,000 discharged?

The hon. member is correct in assuming that the difference between the strength I give him now and the total or net figure that he has there are discharges or are transferred, or have been struck off strength for some other reason.
When it says in the book that men are called up and enrolled, that actually means that those men are enlisted and attested on the army's strength.
I beg my. hon. friend's pardon.

This list which shows enrolments of men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act actually means that these men have been called and have passed the medical examination, and later have been discharged for some reason.
Not all those have been discharged.
The number who are here.
The numbers have not been discharged. That shows the number who have actually been enrolled.

The minister said this afternoon, if I understood him correctly, that there are about 50,000 men called up under the

War Appropriation-Army
National Resources Mobilization Act, commonly known as home defence troops-I understand that they are known as such erroneously-that there are that many men called up under the act who are of a category such that they could be sent overseas, from either coast, to take part in the fighting. In other words, there is an army in Canada of 50,000 of these men who, under the present policy of the government, will never fight unless that fighting takes place on the shores of Canada. This is a question on which there is a very wide difference of opinion between the government and the members of the official opposition. I say that because we believe that these men should be available for fighting wherever they are required. What happened to the Kiska force brings out the point very well. Here we had a force of approximately 5,000 men who were practically all called up uhder the National Resources Mobilization Act. Those men were sent to Kiska. They went there to fight. Everyone has agreed that they carried on in a splendid fashion, and made a very good name for themselves. Of course, there was no actual fighting.
Now, these men have come back to Canada. Kiska has been occupied and these Canadian troops have come back to Canada. I understand they are still on the Pacific coast. Besides that task force there are one or two [DOT]other similar task forces on the coast. All of those troops have been trained for jungle fighting, or in other words, to fight the Japanese. They are thoroughly qualified. I believe some inquiries were made among the units as to whether or not the men were willing voluntarily to go to fight the Japanese, as distinguished from fighting in Europe, and that the majority of men agreed to do so, and said they would be perfectly happy to fight the Japanese. The minister can correct me in that if I am wrong.
But there is the position. Why is it that those men cannot be sent to fight the Japanese? Why do they have to remain in Canada, while the Americans, Australians and New Zealanders are doing the fighting in the Pacific area, and Canada is not represented at all? That seems to me a very unwise position for this nation to be put in. Apparently we are in that position because of the policy of the government in refusing to send any of these men abroad to fight.
The minister said on Friday, referring to the Kiska force, that these men were trained not only for home defence, but for special duty in the Pacific, should action make that necessary and should the decision be made to send them there. Will the minister explain the position with respect to forces such as the
Kiska force? Why cannot that force be sent to fight the Japanese? Why must it stay at home in Canada?
Mr. RALSTON; I wonder if my hon. friend will permit me to get an understanding of his policy. Supposing the Kiska force were to-day general service personnel; would my hon. friend advocate sending them to fight the Japanese?
Yes.
You would?
Yes.
Even with the man-power situation as we have it in Canada, you would advocate that?
Well-
Just a moment.

You have asked me a
question.
You would advocate fighting a third front-Canada fighting the Japanese, too?
The minister cannot evade the question in that way.
I am not evading it.

If the policy of this government were a proper one, and all these 50,000 men were available for fighting, there would be men to send to the Pacific and to Europe. The objection is that you have 50,000 men you cannot send anywhere under your foolish policy.

My hon. friend is generally pretty clear, but I think if I may say so he is not thinking very clearly in this instance. In the first place, at the present time I do not see this parliament authorizing the sending of a force to Japan-
Not to Japan.
To fight the Japanese. The first person to object to it would be the hon. member for York-Sunbury.
I did not say that.
Or his leaders, who may be keener than my hon. friend about reinforce-' rrients. That is one thing they are always talking about, that if these men are there we should leave them for reinforcements.
The minister does not know what is in my mind, at all.

All right. My hon. friend may contradict it if he wishes. These men at
War Appropriation-Army

the present time are, as I have indicated before, a second line of reinforcements. I do not think my hon. friend would be standing on his feet for a single moment advocating the sending of a force just at the moment from Canada to fight the Japanese.
Why did the minister send them to Kiska, then, if they were not to fight?

That was simply a brigade, and that was before we sent our second division to Italy. That was at a time when there was no such activity on the western front such as there is to-day. They were sent there because there was an opportunity to send them to do a job and we did it. My hon. friend seems to think that there are strings on the 50,000 men who are in Canada, that they cannot fight outside Canada. They are trained; they are fit for reinforcement purposes, and they can be sent if the action is taken. They are to-day a potential force for reinforcements as well as for the defence of Canada or for operations on the Pacific.
Why cannot the Kiska force be sent to Europe if the minister does not want to send them to fight the Japanese?

Canada has reached the peak so far as the sending of new capital units overseas is concerned. A year ago we took that stand, and that policy was endorsed by this house. The suggestion has been made to me that I am simply crazy to build up the army, that the army overseas is big enough now. My friend now suggests that we send another brigade in the shape of the Kiska force.
Why cannot they be sent to Europe as reinforcements?

If there is any necessity of sending them overseas, they can be sent if the proper action is taken. I pointed out that at the present time there are in Canada about 60,000 men who will provide feeders for the reinforcement pool overseas. That pool will be filled up again by recruiting. If recruiting does not go on fast enough, then the pool in Canada will be down and we shall have to consider what to do. There is nothing lost through the fact that at the moment these men do not happen to be subject to overseas service.

The plan is to keep these
50.000	fighting men in Canada who have not volunteered for service anywhere, and if next
f\lr, Ralston.]
year more men will be required, others will be sent and these 50,000 will remain here doing nothing.

We must have some men in Canada. These men are serving in Canada and are doing the jobs I have spoken of. If a man wants to volunteer to go overseas, I would rather have him. If we can get it, I would rather have a volunteer army. If the time comes when it is necessary to do something else, then, as I have said to this house before, as far as I am. concerned I shall be ready to make the recommendation. In the meantime these men are trained and they can be used for service in Canada. The}- are available as a second line if action is taken for reinforcements, should the occasion arise.
If the minister wants volunteers to go to Europe and these Kiska men have volunteered to fight the Japanese, why cannot they go to fight the Japanese?

My hon. friend is talking
about these men wanting to fight the Japanese, about our sending a certain force to fight the Japanese. I do not know what my hon. friend is talking about, but I am delighted to hear that the Kiska men are prepared to volunteer for general service.
To fight the Japanese.

I understood that they
volunteered if they were sent as a unit. My hon. friend asks why they" are not sent overseas as reinforcements. They have an opportunity to volunteer and I am sure that some of them are volunteering. As they volunteer they are sent into training.

What does . it cost to keep
these 50,000 men?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think we should have a certain amount of decorum and all remarks should be addressed to the chair.

It costs exactly what it
would cost for any 50,000 men who were needed for service in Canada. For approximately 70,000 men I think the figure would be $100,000,000 a year. That would have to be spent whether it was national resources mobilization personnel or general service personnel so long as the job had to be done here.

The minister has emphasized the necessity of keeping .the units overseas reinforced, and with that I heartily agree. Apparently he is quite satisfied that there are sufficient reinforcements available. Have the

War Appropriation-Army
five divisions overseas been kept up to strength?
I ask that question because on November 25 the following appeared in the Vancouver press:
Indications are that the following changes are being made in the reorganization-
Referring to the army overseas.
1. Withdrawal of troops from the second division to meet requirements in other divisions, thus eliminating that division as a combat force.
It has been reported that some second division units are now classed as training battalions with the task of supplying reinforcements to units on the fighting fronts.
I hope that report is incorrect. The second [DOT]division fought the battle of Dieppe, and this report is to the effect that they aTe not now at full strength as a division and have never been since the battle of Dieppe. Will the minister tell us whether or not that is the situation?

No, it is not true. I heard of that report when I was in England. The second division has a definite task to do in connection with certain operations, and I have no knowledge whatsoever of the second division not being up to strength or not operating as a division. I am sure they are operating as a division.

Just the same as the other
divisions?
Yes.

I do not wish to press the point unduly, but there is something I should like to draw to the minister's attention. He has said that this force of upwards of
70,000	men must be retained to keep the training stream flowing. There has been some criticism of this action in my area and I should like to give the minister an illustration or two. Some young men have bought what have been classed as non-essential businesses such as shoe stores. I know of one case in a town of two thousand where a man bought a business and carried the only up-to-date stock in the community to take care of the farming population. This man was to be forced out of business, and there are other cases I could give the minister. This particular man developed a physical weakness of which no one knew anything, but he received his notice and transportation and had to go to Toronto. He was to be forced to sell his business. The feeling is growing about these cases. People think there could be some reduction in these men who are being retained in the defence army described by the minister. Surely it is not necessary for a married man with three [DOT]children to have to sell his business which
was bought three years before the war started. As I say, there are other cases of which I can give the minister particulars. Apparently if the war goes on one or two more years this force wall still be maintained.

The Department of
National Defence does not call up those men; it simply makes a requisition on the Department of Labour, and national selective service decides whether or not a man is eligible for exemption or deferment. The case cited by my hon. friend does sound like an appealing .one, but it is something the army cannot do much about.

Just so that the minister may have a clear picture, I may say that the young man went to Toronto to the selective service office and explained the circumstances. His whole savings were at stake, but by the time he got back home his notice to report was in the mail and within four days he was to report for service in the army. By a stroke of good luck or otherwise he happened to have some physical1 defect which he had never known of, and that was all that saved him. He had told -the selective service office the position he was in but got nowhere. I give that as one case. You are maintaining a large group, some 70,000 men, in a more or less static state-I know the minister disagrees with that-and when these men plead their case and explain what they are up against to the selective service officers it seems to make no difference. They are called into the army in spite of everything.

Am I to understand from the minister that these men are afraid to go overseas? You can call them by any name you please, but that is what it really amounts to, and they are not from British Columbia. Y^et some of these men who are afraid to go overseas are acting as non-commissioned officers instructing active service men who have volunteered to go overseas.
I do not know of any of them instructing in the training centres.

I do not care where they are instructing. I know that in British Columbia we have men from the province from which the hon. member for York-Sunbury comes, men who have not done an honest day's w'ork in the last six months, who are telling active service men in British Columbia who have volunteered for active service overseas to pick up a cigarette off the sidewalk, or some other order.
War Appropriation-Army
The men from my county all went active.

Right in ,British Columbia we have men from your province.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury)':	Name
them.

I think it is a disgrace that an active service man who has volunteered to go overseas should have one of these men who have not volunteered for service overseas but have two or three stripes telling him what to do. I know what would have 'happened in my battalion if anything of that sort had occurred. If the minister wants instances, I can give them.
I should like to have them.

The minister says that these men are taken into the stream. If they are in a stream, all I can say is that they are trying to run uphill. These men from eastern Canada are not getting infantry training in British Columbia. There are active service men from British Columbia who are building roads and these other men are doing nothing but lying around camps. Some of them could not dig a post-hole in three days. If that is what he calls a streamlined service, I do not know where the minister gets his advice. The minister cannot keep track of all this, I know, but some steps should be taken to see that these men from eastern Canada who have not volunteered for active service are not put in a position to order a volunteer from British Columbia to pick u.p a cigarette from the playground. Yet there they are, sitting around the sidewalk in North Vancouver, and it is a disgrace that these men from eastern Canada are not doing a type of work or undergoing a type of training that would 'be to the good of the country.
I take objection to any suggestion that these men come from my riding.

I think there is a lot to be said about the home defence army. It is most unsatisfactory. I should like to get a broader picture of the general situation. The minister tells us that we have 240,000 troops overseas, and he has said that we are to maintain our army headquarters staff. To most of us this is something new. We do not know what establishment is necessary for an army headquarters staff and all the necessary ancillary troops. Could the minister give us an estimate of the numbers necessary for the present army headquarters staff and ancillary troops? We know how many are required in a division, and I understand that for a 
corps the numbers are almost double those required for the two divisions contained therein. I should like to know the extra percentage required for army headquarters staff and the necessary ancillary troops. I think that has a distinct bearing all the way througft on our reinforcement pool and home defence army.

I explained on Friday to my hon. friend that it is difficult to say how many troops you need when you have an army headquarters, because the corps does provide a proportion of army troops to go to whatever army headquarters are supervising and directing that particular corps. I have not any figures here to-night, but I remember tabling a return showing the number of officers at army headquarters and the number of other ranks required. I do not recall the number of officers, but if I remember correctly the number of additional ranks was shown as something like 7,000 men. I would have to look up the return to be sure of that, but that is my best recollection. The army troops, generally speaking, are provided in large measure by the corps which the army is supervising. The corps provide the army troops for whatever army they may happen to be directing.

Out of present
personnel?
Yes. The army headquarters has no method of recruiting or organizing a unit. It gets its men from a corps and they become army troops and are always under army command.

There are approximately
100,000	men called up under the N.R.M.A., and the present strength is approximately
71,000,	which would indicate that about 29,000 have been discharged or transferred or died.
Or enlisted, or become general service men.
What is the present policy with respect to discharging men in low medical category who have been called up under the N.R.M.A.?
They are discharged when they can be spared. We are endeavouring to have as large a percentage as possible of "A" category men in the army, whether N.R.M.A. or general service.

Is any different policy followed with respect to the discharge of those called up under the N.R.M.A. if they are in a low medical category?

War Appropriation-Army

If it is a matter of requesting a discharge, certainly the general service man would get the preference. That is, where a man would like to get out and is in a low medical category and can be spared the general service man would get the opportunity first. But if it is a case of a man wanting to stay in, the N.R.M.A. man of low medical category would be discharged first.

Can the minister state whether our estimate for necessary reinforcements is at a higher or lower rate than in the last war? In the last war we had a considerable amount of difficulty in maintaining a sufficient flow of reinforcements, and our units were usually below strength. The strength of five battalions would pass as reinforcements through one battalion. Naturally, people are puzzled. They wonder how we are going to maintain a sufficient volume of reinforcements when we have so many men in the armed forces, in the navy, army and air force, and at the same time so many more on the production line.
I beg your pardon.
On the production line. Just exactly how many men have we available for reinforcements in Canada, England, Italy and Egypt? What is the total number, or do you not care to give that information?
I am sorry, I could not give that.
Can you tell us how the estimates compare with the estimates of the last war? Is it higher or lower? It seems to me it must be very much lower than the estimate we had in the last war.

I do not think any comparison can be made. I do not know what the basis was in the last war, but obviously the composition and employment of the forces are entirety different in this war. The forces are entirety different. I do not think any useful or intelligent comparison could be made.
On the other hand, you would not say that the casualties will be lower, surety. You would expect the casualties to be higher, if anything, if we are to have many more Dieppe raids, for instance.
I hope we shall not have any more Dieppe raids.

We have to be prepared, nevertheless. Could the minister say what the policy is in regard to the appointment of officers in the filling of vacancies in the field? Have the commanders the right to fill vacancies of officers in the field by appointing men from
the ranks, as they did in the last war? At that time men were taken from the ranks and given a commission on the field.

I can say to my hon. friend that is a matter which is under discussion at the present moment. There is some discussion as to what is best to do; that is to say, whether an officer who has had officer training should be used when there is a surplus of officers, or whether the appointments should be made directly on the field without further training. The matter is under discussion now, as a matter of fact, with Canadian military headquarters. Obviously there are many advantages in having a man who is battle-trained. He has been a non-commissioned officer, he knows conditions; at the same time there are certain qualifications which are required by commissioned officers which can, I think, best be obtained by longterm training which we endeavour to give them. There is something to be said for using officers when you have thorn rather than making ad hoc appointments on the field. The matter is under consideration.

The minister knows that a lot of hard feeling was caused in the last war by sending green officers over to take charge of men who had had two, three or four years service. I think it took a lot of pressure on the part of the commander in the field before they were given the right to make these appointments on the field. I think further consideration should be given to that.

I happened to be a commander myself on the field in the last war. I remember one or two circumstances at that time, but I always did this. I do not think I ever appointed a man on the field; I recommended him to go back to England and take an officers' training course, if he had all the qualifications and all the equipment that a man should have in order to take that position.
In the early stages of the war there may be men appointed on the field who were not given the chance of officers training.
I know that.

May I suggest to the minister that it might be advantageous and help to clear the picture if he explained briefly to the committee the practice of selecting men to be trained as officers. Only those men who have had a very considerable amount of experience in Canada, or in field units overseas are selected as officers. I have had an oppor-
War Appropriation-Army

tunity in recent months of seeing a considerable number of those who are passing through the officer training period in England, and I do not know of anyone-I may be open to correction in this-who has come to the officer training centres from the field forces in England in recent months who has not had field experience. They are not building up their reserves any more with inexperienced people from civilian life. They are building them up from men who have been in the service a minimum length of time under the regulations and who have complete training or experience overseas. They are men who have trained in the arm of the unit from which they come.
Go to a barber college and get a commission.

I have one or two questions to ask the minister with respect to reinforcements. He stated on Friday that although we were maintaining our army headquarters we had only one corps, and that the other corps would be supplied by Britain. My first question is, if our three divisions are in action I presume that the Canadian pool to which he referred would supply the reinforcements for our own divisions.
Correct.
Second, in the event of an invasion of the continent, can the minister give us any estimate of the percentage of reinforcements that might be necessary within the first two weeks?

I would not attempt to give any estimate of that kind. I say to my hon. friend that provision has been made for reinforcements on a scale which is regarded as adequate. We had exactly the same situation in Sicily. This is not the first time, you know. We had an invasion in Sicily and we sent reinforcements which were regarded as adequate for the first two weeks, and much longer than that.

We have been told that there is a reinforcement pool in Canada and a pool in England, and if the pool runs out in England it will be reinforced from the pool in Canada. It would take a considerable time to move these troops from Canada to England, and if we have very heavy casualties in the first two weeks or month of the invasion, then I think the people of this country would like to be assured that we have sufficient reinforcements available immediately to take care of the situation. I should like to ask the minister if he can give that assurance.
I think I can.

The criticisms that I have heard wherever I have gone regarding the home defence army is that we are sending men overseas with considerably short periods of training, and we shall probably be sending others if the emergency arises, with still shorter periods of training, while we have in the home defence army men who have had much longer years of service and more years of training. That is the chief criticism that I have heard regarding the home defence army in my ramblings around the country. The minister has indicated that the government does not think it advisable at the present time to have Canadians engaged in war with Japan but that our forces should be concentrated in the war in Europe. I think it is generally understood that the war with Japan will continue possibly for some years after we hope the war in Europe will have finished. Has the government formulated any plans regarding the use of Canadians against the Japanese when the war in Europe has been completed. That requires, I am told, a Large number of attendants, men who know Japanese, know Japanese customs, men who have worked with the army. I understand the Americans are doing a great deal in the way of training men for that work. Is anything of that kind being contemplated in Canada at the present time?

In the first place, what I said with regard to Japan or what I wanted to say was, that no commitments have been made at the present time as to the nature or extent of Canada's participation in the war against * Japan. At the same time I wish to say, as I said last year, that the army recognizes fully that we are at war with Japan- and we are making plans accordingly. I cannot give my hon. friend any statement with regard- to policy.

I believe there is a good deal
of uneasiness among certain people with regard to the army's role in strikes. I was in Shaw-inigan Falls at the time of the strike, having been invited by -the unions to go and speak, and while there I found quite a number of soldiers who had been- sent from Famham. They were French-Canadian soldiers, it is true, but they were parading the streets intimidating the workers and they did not create the best impression upon the. people. I do not think it is the best thing for the morale of the soldiers, who believe there is a greater enemy for them to fight than their fellow Canadians at Shawinigan Falls. Who ordered the soldiers there? In the Montreal strike of policemen and firemen there were, I understand, one thousand men sent from Farnham.

War Appropriation-Army
It is true they were not paraded but were kept in barracks, but here again they were men who had been sent for the purpose of dealing with the strike. Many of these men expressed regret at being used for that purpose. The reserve army is another organization that was ready for action in connection with the Montreal strike. A colonel-I cannot say what his name is-said after the strike that he was sorry he did not get the chance to come to grips with the strikers. The reserve army officers, especially some of the older men are through and' through reactionary. They still think of the good old days. I would suggest that some of the older officers of perhaps thirty-five or forty released from active service, be placed in the reserve army instead of having men of between fifty and sixty, old men, who as I said before still think of the good old days. They are jingoes; they do not understand the new spirit of Canada and of the world. There have been a number of occasions when men in the reserve army have been told, "It is true the danger of attack is over, but after the war we may have to be used in case of emergency." What emergency is contemplated? We are not planning for trouble. If we mean to plan for a peaceful post-war there is no necessity to arouse people who join the reserve army by telling them that they may be used in case of emergency.

Are all officers liable for
overseas service, or is it necessary for an officer to volunteer for overseas service? Are officers still trained for the reserve army?

All officers are liable for overseas service. Do I understand the hon. member to ask whether officers are still being trained for the overseas army? Does he mean, are reserve army officers being trained at Brockvillc?
Yes.
I cannot be sure, but I think that is so. I have not inquired in the last month. There is a very small number.

The question I have to ask is along the line of that asked by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White). What is the policy with respect to non-commissioned officers and commissioned serving in Canada who desire to proceed overseas? Is it necessary, in order to proceed overseas, to revert to the rank of noncommissioned officer or to take a lower rank if one is a commissioned officer? Second, with respect to N.R.M.A. forces, is it not true that whole units of these forces have volunteered their services generally, provided the
unit be not split up, and that if it was necessary to send them to any theatre of war, provided they could be sent as a unit, they were prepared to proceed on that basis? I think myself, that, with respect to the N.R.M.A. forces, they are receiving a good deal of abuse which they do not deserve. We must remember that when the war broke out the great majority of these boys were young fellows who were roaming the streets, who had very little to fight for, and with absolutely no knowledge of the military set-up. But they were called up to report for military duty, and in many cases they were sent to camps where, after considerable training received since going into the services, they have had names hurled at them and everything done to discourage them, though they might have tended otherwise to take their place in the legitimate army and proceed overseas. I find no fault with them.
The Minister of National Defence, in summing up the general situation at the time he began his report to the house at this session, made it quite clear that it was necessary to maintain in Canada an army for emergency purposes, that it was necessary to fortify our coasts at both ends of the country, and many of the men of that army who get such a ribbing have been doing duty in outlying sections of the country and have undergone considerable hardship. They have been posted out there and have had to stick to their posts, and they have done a very useful service. There is no doubt about that. At the last session I said, and I say it again, that anyone who takes the position in this house that every man in uniform in Canada during the past three years should have been routed overseas is taking a very unrealistic position.
The main difficulty we have had to contend with in the past two and a half years has been to get something overseas for those who were already there. Shipping has been our difficulty. And what was the soldier in Britain doing during the past two and a half years which the soldier in Canada was not doing? He was kicking his heels waiting for action. One of the main difficulties facing those charged with the responsibility of maintaining the morale of the troops over there was to keep them busy doing nothing until such time as there was somewhere to send them into action. I hate to sit back listening to armchair generals who are quite comfortably seated in Canada, prepared to carry on the war until the last worker is killed. I am not interested in that line of argument. I
War Appropriation-Army

think these men are badly abused.. They were boys picked up on the street who knew nothing but starvation under the regime of those who now take the position that they should all be prepared to die for a country that disinherited them while those persons were themselves in power. I think these boys have performed a useful service and do not deserve the names that have been hurled at them and the abuse they have received during the time they have been doing a very valuable job in Canada, standing, on guard on all our coasts, while at the same time unit after unit have been volunteering, provided they could go overseas as a unit. The position taken by many in the house is completely unjustified, and I am certain of this, because these boys, by and large, are the brothers or sons of men who to-night are in Sicily doing the fighting. If the time comes when they need reinforcements over there, when our army is in action, there will not be found any difficulty getting most of them to volunteer to go there.
I think national defence has been well advised, although I do not agree with them in every thing, in maintaining that army on that basis until such time as it is needed over there. To suggest that this force should have been sent to Britain during the past two years, to load upon the British government the burden of feeding and looking after them, was a completely unrealistic position to take. I have sufficient confidence in those boys as Canadians to believe that when the time comes they will make their contribution where it is most needed.
I did not intend to speak at any length at this time. There are many things that could be said with respect to the army overseas, but I do not think this is the time to say them. However, I should like the minister to answer the question with respect to officers and non-commissioned officers who desire to proceed overseas, as to whether or not they are compelled to relinquish their rank. I know there are officers in Canada who are anxious to get over, who have volunteered from the army to the air force, from the army to the paratroops and so on, in an attempt to get a shift out of Canada, but they have been held here, I do not know for what reason.

With regard to the necessity for a non-commissioned officer or an officer to revert in order to go overseas, there is an agreement with Canadian military headquarters and with the army that a certain proportion-it is a small proportion-of reinforcement troops can be particular ranks; I think there are some sergeants and even some as high as warrant officers class 2, but not a great many. To answer my hon. friend's question directly, it is not an absolute rule [Mr. Gillis.J
that every non-commissioned officer has to take off his stripes before he goes overseas; it all depends on the need for non-commissioned officers over there and of course to some extent on the qualifications of the man here. With regard to officers, captains have been taken as such, though not a great many. Generally speaking, we would very much prefer to have subalterns there, in order that they might work up, but occasionally captains are taken.
With regard to N.R.M.A. personnel volunteering as units, that is a very attractive proposition for the recruiting officer; it means that he fills up his month's quota pretty quickly if he can get a whole battalion to volunteer, but I may say it is a headache for the administrative officers because it means arranging to have that unit go overseas as a unit. The formations overseas are already constituted, and in order to keep faith the unit volunteering it might be necessary to break up another unit which has been overseas for a good while. That has never been done, although offers of that kind have been made. Generally . speaking, the matter is explained to the men in the unit. We endeavour to keep them together as much as possible, and we have had arrangements under which platoons and even larger subunits of the unit have gone over together. We endeavour to keep theili together in the reinforcement centre, but I do not know of any case in which an entire unit composed of N.R.M.A. personnel has ever volunteered and gone over as a unit. As my hon. friend can see, it would mean adding to the capital overseas, which in turn would mean adding to the reinforcement liability here, and putting an extra unit on a formation that is already complete.

I agree with the minister. I was not arguing the merits or demerits of the scheme; I was trying to correct the impression created by some hon. members and others that the N.R.M.A. men in Canada were slackers, that they wore the uniform but did not want to fight. That impression has been created, and I agree that the mechanics of the situation as outlined by the minister are such that it is not possible to do these things. It is only natural that after serving for two or three years most of these boys should want to go overseas. They are not all slackers.

I want to support the thought that has been expressed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. Coming as we do from the Atlantic coast, he and I have had an opportunity of coming in contact with the men who have been serving in the coastal defence units. This question has been raised on more than one occasion, and some criticism

War Appropriation-Army
has been offered in regard to the so-called home service men. The same criticism was expressed during the last war when, as now, - men were obliged to carry out duties which were considered necessary on both the eastern and western coasts. I am glad to join with the hon. member for Cape Breton South in voicing my objection to the opinion so often expressed by unthinking members of this house as well as by citizens at large, that the man serving in the home forces is not performing a necessary duty. On more than one occasion the minister has expressed his appreciation of these men on the floor of this chamber. Last year he stated that the men on home service were absolutely necessary; and we all know, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, that for the past three or four years they have been receiving training. Perhaps it has not been as extensive as the training given those who were proceeding overseas, but very important training has been given our home service men to prepare them to take their place either overseas or in defence of the shores of our country, if that should be necessary. I thought I should like to add my word of commendation for those who are obliged, quite often against their own wish and desire, to serve on our eastern and western shores.
If the hon. member would permit a question, why are they obliged to serve in Canada?
That is a question that perhaps neither the hon. member nor I can answer. I leave that to those with more experience in these matters.

I wonder if the minister would deal with the matter I brought up, concerning the statement which has been made to me not once but many times, that scattered across Canada-I mentioned Petawawa as an instance-there are said to be a very considerable number of officers who apparently are not attached to units or taking courses: perhaps *"unattached" is the proper term to use, but they are officers who do not appear to have any definite work to do. They are to be seen not only at Petawawa but at Vancouver and various other places in Canada. To what extent is that an accurate statement?

I cannot tell my hon. friend to what extent it is an accurate statement. I did say that we had a reserve of officers, so that we are pretty comfortably off. As a matter of fact, at the present moment an arrangement is under consideration for the employment of quite a large number of officers, which will reduce that surplus very considerably. I am surprised to hear my hon. friend suggesting that these officers are simply in camps, unemployed. I had understood that they were taking these advanced courses and refresher courses, not only at Brockville but at the schools of instruction being held at the advanced training centres as well. I can only say to my hon. friend that I shall inquire about the matter at once and shall be glad to give the committee the information. I know what my hon. friend wants is action, not information, but I shall try to give the information and get the action as well.
Then has the minister any information to give the committee with regard to deserters, how many there are, how many are being pursued, and how many he anticipates will be apprehended?

Could I make a note of that and give the information to my hon. friend to-morrow? I have,in mind that there is pretty nearly a constant number. There are recaptures; then somebody else deserts, and so on. I cannot tell my hon. friend the rate of inflow or output.
Would the minister deal with it as far as possible, so far as their origins are concerned? That is to say, would he tell us from what part of the Canadian active army they come?
According to districts?
Yes.

While we are under this heading I would draw to the attention of the minister the case I took up with him some little time ago. I am quite satisfied with the action in that part of it in which the minister interested himself, but I must point out that if this case is typical and if the information I have is correct, then there would appear to be many men in the home defence army-if I am using the correct term-who are receiving very little military training, and most of whose time is taken up in working for private employers.
I have a letter from the parents of a young boy who was inducted into the army on March 8, 1943. He was taken first to Little Mountain barracks, and was there for only a short time when he was sent to Victoria. He then went to Alberni where he worked for three months in the bush. His parents state that while there he was pulling telephone poles through the bush with ropes, for a private contractor. That lasted for three months. The rather peculiar circumstance in this instance is that the parents of the boy say that an army officer had said he was not strong enough for ordinary military training.
War Appropriation-Army
Is this the boy who went to the hospital in Vancouver?

Yes, he went to hospital, mentally deranged. Further, after working at Alberni for three months he came back to Victoria, and from there went to Patricia Bay, where he had about a week's training. Then he came home to Vancouver for a week's leave, I believe. From there he was sent to Port Hardy, where he was handed a pick and shovel and started to work at digging ditches. Whether this was for a private contractor or for the army I cannot say, nor could his parents.
He worked there for a while ,and then was sent to Vernon, staying there for a little more than a week. From there he was sent to work for the Canadian National Railways at Blue River.
