For a person who is not physically strong, track maintenance work is one of the heaviest types of work a person could do, and is particularly hard for a person who is not used to that type of work. He was there for a short time when his parents were notified that he was back again at Little Mountain barracks, mentally deranged.
How many of the men in the home defence army are doing work for private employers such as the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway, or other employers of that type? During the three months the boy was at Port Alberni was he doing army work, or working for a private employer? These are questions to which the fathers and mothers of young lads in the army would like to receive answers.

I cannot tell my hon. friend how many are detailed. It is some time since I looked at the order in council. There was an order in council providing that personnel under the National Resources Mobilization Act could be detailed in units or subunits for civilian work. Then there was a provision under which they could be given leave and could go to a private employer. I am sorry I cannot tell my hon. friend as to how many are in each class, but I shall have the information to-morrow.
Although my hon. friend did mention that feature of the matter in his letter, I must say that I do not think I dealt with it, because I w'as more concerned with the boy's health, and as to whether he was going to get along all right. I do not think I dealt with that matter, did I?

No; the minister dealt very quickly with the matter of the boy's health, and the other feature was not men-

tinned in the correspondence which passed between us. Had it been explained to my satisfaction I would not have bothered mentioning it to-night, because I discuss in the house only those questions which I cannot settle in another way.
Did the hon. member give me the boy's name?
I have given the name to the minister.
What we wish to do is find out the circumstances under which he did that particular job, and also the number of men in that class.
I want to know if this boy was working for a private contractor for three months when he was at Port Alberni, and how this affects other men in the army.

I believe there was an order in council authorizing the detailing of men to do railway work at a time when the railways vcere short of help. I believe that would be the class in which he would come, but I shall look into the matter.
Under what arrangements do men work for private employers? Are they paid by the army or by the employers?

I am sorry I have not the order in council with me. However, if it is the same as the regulation with respect to work on farms, it w'ill be recalled that they were paid a flat rate per day, depending on the zone in which the work was done. However, I shall find out about this particular man, because he will be representative of the class.
The matter is not confined to that order in council. Just a few. days ago I received a letter from London, Ontario, protesting-
My hon. friend has extended his constituency.

I think I am elected to represent Canada as a whole, with the exception of the constituency of the Minister of Pensions and National Health. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) looks after that.
In this particular case a charge was made that through some arrangement with the authorities in that area carpenters were released and were employed on jobs, thereby displacing regular carpenters.

Where did this happen?

War Appropriation-Army

London, Ontario. There was
considerable controversy with selective service in the matter. No progress was made, and it was suggested I should take it up in the house. I have written the department, but have not yet received a reply. That seems to be a pretty general thing all the way through.

Supplementary to the question raised by the hon. member for Yale with respect to surplus officers throughout the country, I understand the minister's department conducted a survey during the past months to see how many such officers were in Canada who were not now rendering useful service. When the minister brings down his answer, would he give us the number of these officers, and also the number who have been discharged? I know several officers who have been notified of their discharges without any reasons being given. No doubt some of them had passed the age limit, but the newspapers have carried articles about this.

My hon. friend refers to
officers being discharged without any reasons being given. I am very particular about that, and if he knows of any case I wish he would bring it to my attention. There is a most strict procedure laid down. I try to see the files myself. I would be disappointed to know if there were such cases. If there are any I should like to know of them for administrative purposes. An officer who has served and served well is certainly entitled to know the reason why he is being reverted to reserve status.

One man showed me
his papers from the department and they did not give any reason. I know this man personally and I believe he is over age, but I shall let the minister have his name.

I appreciate that there
are officers who are over age and are being retired, and there are others who cannot be usefully employed, but I wonder whether the department has considered the advisability of an opportunity to resign being given to some officers who are now usefully employed. Perhaps it could be intimated to these men that their resignations would meet with approval. There are three or four cases that come to my mind at this time. These men held good positions or conducted businesses before they entered the army three or four years ago. They have done an excellent and worth-while job in Canada in training men for overseas. In each case the man is a veteran of the last war in which he served with distinction. I believe they would all be glad to return to civilian life and make way for other men less fortunate
or for men who are coming back from overseas. They hesitate to take the step because of the reflection that might be cast upon their devotion to duty. I feel sure these men would be glad to tender their resignations if it were indicated to them that that would be agreeable and acceptable to the government and that there would be no question of their patriotism.
There is another matter concerning the treatment given to officers who are retired because they have reached the age limit-I understand the principle is that these men must be retired unless a certificate is made to the adjutant-general that another suitable man is not available-and to officers who are asked to retire for other reasons. In the first case the officer is given a gratuity on retirement of one day's pay for every twelve days of service, or one month's pay for each year of service, whereas the officer who is asked to retire receives only the bare gratuity of one month's pay. I consider that this is an injustice.
An officer may be a veteran of the last war, he may have served Canada for three years, but when he is retired he is given a gratuity of one month's pay. A brother officer may be-retired because of age, and if he has served the same time he will receive a gratuity of three months' pay. If I have not a true appreciation of the facts perhaps the minister will correct me, but if I am correct then I think this matter should be reconsidered. Personally I do not think it is fair to have a man serve two or three years and then be told that he is out on thirty days' notice and will receive only one month's gratuity.

The first point raised by my hon. friend was with regard to permission being given to officers to resign. I have no doubt that the officer in question would prefer to revert to reserve status because, if he resigned, he would have to resign his commission, whereas if he reverts he could go back on the active list again if the occasion arose. I am sure that the boards which discuss these matters would consider that point in those cases where officers cannot be advantageously employed. I shall see that the idea is transmitted to the boards.
The other point raised by my hon. friend was with regard to the apparent discrepancy between the case of the man who had reached sixty years of age and was being retired a,nd the case of the man who had not reached that age and was being retired because he was not advantageously employable. There is a difference between those two cases which may sound technical. The man who has reached sixty years of age has a job and most likely
War Appropriation-Army

he is fit to fill that job. The job is there for him but suddenly because of age he is out. That regulation was not in force at the time he entered the service and it was thought that he should have some compensation. The other man had held his position subject to his being retired if he could not be advantageously employed. That situation came about and he svas paid a gratuity. As I say, the distinction may be somewhat technical, but there is a real distinction between the two. However, the matter is under active consideration, and I shall take note of what my hon. friend has said with regard to it.

The Minister of National Defence for Air made the statement the other day that negotiations were going on between the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F. with a view to allowing Canadians who had enlisted in the R.A.F. since the beginning of the war to transfer to the R.C.A.F., and I was wondering whether similar discussions might be going on with respect to Canadians who had enlisted in the British army at the outbreak of the war and might want to transfer to the Canadian army. The two men that I have particularly in mind enlisted in the British army in a specialist capacity on the understanding that when the Canadians came over they would be transferred to the Canadian army; but from that day to this, despite their best efforts, they have never been permitted) to transfer to Canadian forces, despite the fact that they are Canadians. Are similar negotiations going on with respect to the army such as the minister for air indicated were going on as between the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F.?

Very recently there arose a case of one particular officer, and there was a discussion tljen on general principles. I shall make inquiries and see how far those discussions went. The British pay us a compliment in wanting to keep Canadian officers when they get them, and they do not meet with any great enthusiasm the suggestion that they transfer. I will see how far the discussions have progressed.

A soldier in the Canadian army on discharge receives $65 as clothing allowance. I understand that in the United States on discharge the soldier receives from $100 to $300. Has this government any intention of increasing pur allowance?
I think my hon. friend is mixing up two things. The $100 to $300 in the United States is what they call mustering-out pay, a sort of war service gratuity.
It is the same thing.
No; the $65 clothing allowance is paid to enable a man on discharge to get a civilian outfit. I presume the United States also have a clothing allowance for their army.
And the Canadian soldier gets one month's pay as well.
Yes. The United States army, I presume, has also a clothing allowance, but what it amounts to I do not know.

Can the minister tell us how many recruits have enlisted voluntarily month by month during the past year? There is no doubt that immediately after the passing of the National Resources Mobilization Act, recruiting for the air force and navy speeded up; I do not know how it affected recruiting for the army. But the government have now got a tiger by the tail, and do not know what to do with it.
I have another question to ask while the minister is looking up those figures. I have no doubt that to-morrow he will answer my question on the orders of the day in connection with the speech made by Major-General Chisholm in Toronto from which I quoted. There are one or two other quotations I should like to give now from that same speech. He is reported to have said:
Too many women are bringing up too many boys on women's values, without relation to their obligation to the community. The result is that the army has to do a lot of unnecessary "growing up" of recruits.
I think that is a terrible castigation of our womenfolk. I do not blame the women for that at all. I do blame one woman who used to be a member of this House of Commons and used to rise in this house and ask for the cadet corps to be wiped out, and who now belongs to the national socialist party, and who was always asking in this house to have the defence estimates reduced to one dollar, and so on. But there were also many other gentlemen now sitting on the opposite side who in years gone by refused to have the defence estimates raised. It was that sort of thing, the education given by such people- and I include some of our friends on the opposite side-that is responsible for what Major-General Chisholm complains of. Then they were for no commitments; there was no danger at all; they were isolationists, and so on. So I say you cannot blame the women of Canada for the consequences.
This national selective service is now a half idea: it is neither fish nor fowl. As I say, the government have a tiger by the tail

4T3
iVar Appropriation-Army
and do not know what to do with it. Just imagine trying to put 75,000 of these zombies on a boat going overseas. What good would they do? And would you ever get them there?
Major-General Chisholm makes another pertinent statement. He says:
The Canadian army has had to reject large numbers of men, and the British, United States and Canadian armies have found it expensive to train men who find it difficult to reorient themselves from a position of thinking of the privilege of the individual to the general security of the group.
Do they discharge them for that reason or just let them sit here at home? Is there any educational process being applied in that situation? What are we going to do with these people? It is all' very well to continue to talk about having these people, but something should be done about it.
I see recruiting posters all around the country addressed to the women, and by the way these are the women of whom Major-General Chisholm says:
In times of stress, such as war, women became a liability.
As I say, these posters are appealing to the women of the country to join up and release men for active service. It is true that we want more women to release men for overseas service. But I ask, why should we appeal to women to release men for overseas service when we have so many men here who are doing nothing at all? The minister said that they are on non-operational duty. The hon. member for Fraser Valiev told us what these men are doing in British Columbia. I am glad that there are none from my riding among those he spoke of in British Columbia. But that is a situation that has been brought about by the National Resources Mobilization Act. It is simply ridiculous. The' enforcement of the act is all crazy. I know a number of men in the army who would have been far more useful in Canada, and we have people taking their place here who would be far more useful in the army. I know of many instances like that. We have no national mobilization or selective service in Canada at all. We have the National Resources Mobilization Act which is neither one thing nor the other. A little while ago there was a certain amount of pressure brought to bear on these people to have them go active, but you cannot get them to go active any more. What we have to do now is to depend on recruits. Suppose you need these people and you have to bring in an act to make them go active so that they may be sent to any place in the world. That will be all right, but what
good are they going to be? That is the situation. I have finished my statement and I hope the minister will answer the other question to-morrow.

In reference to Major-General Chisholm's speech I have told my hon. friend I would reply to-morrow. I do not think I can add anything to what I have already said other than to correct my hon. friend once more with regard to the employment of these men in Canada. My hon. friend says they are doing nothing. I told him what they are doing as reported to me.
I get these reports from the district officers commanding. The hon. member for Fraser Valley seems to have a situation in his part of the country which needs to be corrected.
I am going to have somebody on the job and if he will give me some information about it we shall see that it is cleaned up. These men are not loafing by any means. The work is there for them to do and they are doing it. I am glad to have this opportunity to endeavour at least to dispel in the minds of those who will listen and who will accept the fact as it is given to me, the idea that these men are doing nothing, because my information is that as operational troops and as nonoperational troops in these two service units they are doing work that has to be done by somebody, and would have to be done by general service personnel if these men were not available.
Shall the item carry?

I should like to ask this question: Have we in Canada men who are being discharged all the time, as Major-General Chisholm says here, because they cannot reorient themselves from the possibility of thinking of the privilege of the individual rather .than the general security of the group? He says they are being discharged, and I am perfectly sure that I could give instances.
They are going back to civil life. My hon. friend says they are needed there. The country' is not going to lose them because they are being discharged from the army.

Are they useful, and could they take the place of some of these fellows who are doing service in Canada who might very well do service in other places? That work could very well be done by men in category "E."

What do you suggest, keep the men-
War Appropriation-Army

May I finish before the minister replies? We have men being discharged from the army for mental reasons. The minister is laughing. I will take the laugh off his face in a minute. Men are being discharged from the army for mental reasons. They have been taken into the army as category "A." They are then examined by psychiatrists and are then discharged for emotional instability, constitutional inadequacies, as psychopaths and mental defectives. They are placed in category "E" and are not pensionable. They could be doing useful work. Are they to be a charge on the community for the rest of their lives? They have that stigma attached to their names for the rest of their lives. Could they not be kept in the army to take the place of some other men in category "A" who are doing work that these discharged men could do? One does not need very much intelligence or be very bright to do some of these jobs. I think these men could very well be used for that purpose. You are going to have a lot of these men on your hands, and something should be done about the matter. I do not think the thing is very well run at all.

I can say to my hon. friend that I have seen quite a number of these men that he speaks of and who he says do not have to be very bright. I am thinking of the Longue Point depot, for instance. I think some of these men and women would qualify as members of parliament. I do not think they are devoid of grey matter.

We have been talking all around item number one. Last year the item amounted to $8,832,000. This year it is $16,000,000. I should like to ask the minister why the item is almost double this year and just what it covers.

The increase is due to the fact that we have very much increased the number of civilian employees as we have *decreased the service personnel. The total increase, as my hon. friend will see, amounts to about $7,000,000. Soldier's were replaced by civilians, and that accounts for about $2,000,-
000.	Included in that also are the hourly paid employees who were included elsewhere in 1943 and 1944. That amounts to $3,000,000. In other words, that $3,000,000 is taken from another place and is cut off another item.
Do the people who are employed wear uniforms?

No. I inquired about this item. I said, how is it we increased the pay and allowances of the civilian employees, and increased the pay and allowances of the army and still, at the same time, were reducing the
"Mr. Halston.]
army? As a matter of fact, I found the actual decrease in the pay and allowances of other ranks is $17,000,000 as compared with 1943-44, but various increases total $24,000,000 altogether in pay and allowances. Of this, $17,000,000 is accounted for by the decrease in pay of other ranks, while the increase in the pay of civilians is about $7,000,000. Therefore, on this basis, you will see there is a saving of about $10,000,000. There is one more item, reclassification of positions, $552,000, which is another part of the $7,000,000. The growth of army administration shows an increase of $2,000,000, due to increased number of employees.
Is that a reclassification of civilian positions?
Civil Service reclassification. Reclassifications are taking effect now, a certain number every year.
They did not get the cost-of-living bonus.
That is a reclassification of twenty-three hundred positions since the 1943-44 estimates were prepared.. The total is $552,000 altogether.
Shall the item carry?

Can the minister give the committee some information with regard to the organization that is being set up to take over administrative duties in reoccupied countries? I have had several inquiries made by officers who are at the present time in the army in Canada. Some of these men, it would seem to me, are well suited by their experience for suc-h work. Is it an international organization that is being set up, of which Canada supplies so much, or is Canada setting up an organization of her own for that purpose? Can the minister give the committee some information with regard to that organization?

I have a memorandum here, but I shall not read it all. The situation in North Africa was the first immediate situation which required attention in the way of civil administration. The necessity for some measure of temporary jurisdiction being established by the military over the large number of civilians in territories freed from enemy control was indicated. The commanders in chief first appointed officers for that purpose. These were known as civil administrators or military governors, as the case might be, and the work was carried on by military personnel. The civil affairs officers were employed, first, on staffs of formations and, second, as civil

War Appropriation-Army
affairs detachments. I remember, if I may interject the observation, that a member of the tariff board of Canada, Major Hebert, is a member of the civil affairs administration in Italy at the present time. During an advance the formation staffs -tackle the problems as they arise, and detachments are established when important towns or centres are taken. The detachment then guards every t-own or centre under direction from formation headquarters and in cooperation with the local authorities if available.
Following on .the opening of -civil affairs schools in Britain and the United States it was decided to conduct a two-months' course along similar lines in Canada and we have established a course at the Royal Military college. The first group of twenty-four ^officers graduated recently. That is a joint undertaking covering the three services, the Department of External Affairs acting in an advisory capacity. A number of Canadian officers overseas have attended the civil affairs school in England and a few have taken the course in the United States. Our people who have established the school at the Royal Military college and are in charge of it have been at the school in England and also at the school in the United States to make themselves familiar with the syllabus provided and to ascertain the different kinds of training given in Britain and America. Canadian officers will be available for the staffs of Canadian formations for work at various times in which there is intermixture of British and American. The civil affairs administration is a temporary measure to be maintained in any locality only so long as it is required.
My hon. friend has inquired with regard to an officer friend, and I may tell him that commanding officers were asked to make recommendations of those who had qualifications, who had some knowledge of municipal affairs, town planning or general administration, or public utilities, water works, light systems and matters of that kind. Linguists are also useful, though not unless they have some training or experience in connection with civil administration. As my hon. friend quite understands, there is very little in the way of military training given, because it is a military officer who is being dealt with. If anyone in whom my hon. friend is interested wishes to do so, anyone who might be qualified for this work, he ought to apply to his D.O.C. and have his name sent in.
What numbers does the minister expect to obtain-scores or hundreds?

I do not know how long we shall maintain the school here. There is
also a school in England. I expect there will be two or three more courses, and the number may be a hundred or more.
Will the minister give those figures about which I inquired?

Last session the Minister of National Defence for the army laid before the house a schedule recording pay and allowances for all ranks. It would surprise members to know of the different inequalities that exist, starting with lieutenant-colonel and major right down to private. The return showed a rate per- day of SI HO and in some cases SI .50, and it went straight across the blueprint, giving the total for the year. There were a great many inequalities in that schedule of the lower-paid men, and I should like to find out what is being done to remove them. The minister for the navy and . the minister for air followed and gave a similar statement, a blueprint which was published in Hansard. It caused a great deal of dissatisfaction among the returned men and those overseas, because some received certain allowances, while others did not get anything. It may not be altogether in the minister's department, but I think some explanation ought to be given while the minister's estimates are before us, because the same thing applies throughout. Young men have joined up from the high schools of the country. The high schools of Toronto alone have given (XK) men in casualties to the air force. I suggest, therefore, that the inequalities that appear in the schedule should be removed.
In the matter of allowances, some receive them and others do not. Section 11, subsection 3, of the Pension Act applies to the army, and last week a deputation appeared before the board of control in connection with this matter. One section relates to the necessitous circumstances of soldiers coming home. They do not get a grant at all and some are practically on the street. That section as applied to the army means simply charity. As I say, a deputation appeared before the board of control of Toronto last Thursday, and I will send the information to the minister. As regards clothing allowances, the $65 for a returned man should be marked up. The officers have been marked up and I do not see why the privates and non-commissioned officers should be forgotten. They are largely doing good work in the camps. I receive many letters from the returned men. There are many in my constituency and throughout Toronto. I do not like to bother the minister, but I hope that- something will be done to remove the inequalities between the private soldier and the non-commissioned officers as
War Appropriation-Army

compared with the men at the top of the ladder. There should be an announcement, and I hope it will come shortly, with regard to this whole matter, which will give to these people who are coming home some additional allowance for clothing and so on. The minister gave an elaborate statement last year about the matters to which I have referred, and I should like to find out if anything additional in allowance is to be done about the large number of men who are coming back from the front.

What I shall try to do is to get the statement made last year and make a comparison to see how much ironing out there has been of the inconsistencies in the different classes. I believe a substantial change has been effected since that schedule was filed. I should like to see what it looks like this year. We might prepare a new schedule and see how it compares with the old. With regard to the other matter, rehabilitation and the announcement of a policy with respect to what assistance is to be given, that announcement will be made in due course. I will take note of what my hon. friend says and see if we cannot get a new statement to see how it compares with the old, and what suggestion my hon. friend has to make.

Regarding pay and allowances, there is a good deal of complaint in the camps about leave, and the amount of money the soldier must pay to get home over the week-end. This applies to Camp Borden and many other camps, but little is done about it. The other day in Toronto we had an announcement by Major-General Chisholm which has caused a great deal of dissension and dissatisfaction in the Toronto district among women whose men are at the front or at the camps. Something should be done to find out from the railway companies what they intend to do with regard to a reduction of fares at week-ends for men at the camps. As you know, Mr. Chairman, down to the end of 1940 the railways had made more money than during the entire four and a half }rears of the last war. Surely something should be done by the government and the minister to see that these men are allowed cheaper fares to get home.
Apparently there is a rule now in force that the men are not allowed to write letters to the newspapers about these matters. If that rule applies to privates and non-commissioned officers it should apply also to Major-General Chisholm, who in his talk has caused a great deal of disunity among the families of our soldiers. If it were not for the women who

are doing such magnificent work at home, I doubt if we would have had such success as we have had in connection with recruiting. I hope the rule will apply to Major-General Chisholm and the rest of those at the top who are spreading these rumours about leaves and doing a great deal to hurt recruiting.

I do not want to hold up this resolution, but I should like an answer from the minister with respect to the low-category men who are discharged after having been called up under the mobilization act, or who have returned from overseas as casualties. I do not know whether the information is correct, but I have had at least two letters from military district No. 6, written by men who recently returned from overseas. They complain that the camp is literally blocked with category "C2" men, who are performing no useful service in the camp.
Is this depot at Halifax?

Yes. I have received complaints from men who feel that perhaps they could make a better contribution outside, since they are not fit for regular military duties. That complaint also has come from other places, but the two specific complaints I have had came from military district No. 6. I should like to find out from the minister just what is the policy of the department when a man is boarded, his catgeory is lowered and he is classified as unfit for regular military service. What is he assigned to do in the military district; what duties is he required to carry out, or what service does he perform when he is kept in the army? Would it not

War Appropriation-Army
be 'better to discharge that man and send him out so that he might be able to make a useful contribution in some civilian capacity? I think it would be good business if men like that were routed' 'back to civilian life and given an opportunity to rehabilitate themselves now, before we have the general demobilization. I think it is a mistake to keep any large number of men of this kind in any camp.

I must confess that I agree with my hon. friend. Of course there are some jobs, such as orderlies and things of that kind, in which low-category men can be usefully employed, but. generally speaking I see no point at all in keeping a man of that kind in the army, unless he is absolutely essential and no one else can be obtained to do the work. I indicated that our depots are very full at the present time, though the number of men in them, is going down quite rapidly. However, in talking with my colleague, the Minister of Pensions and National Health, I have inquired into the matter pretty carefully, and I may tell my hon. friend that one reason which is given to me is that the procedure fol-* lowed this time in connection with the discharge of a man is really terrific, in the number of forms that have to be filled out and the examinations that have to be gone through. You may ask why. Well, it is for the purpose of seeing to it that pensionability or otherwise is established at the start, instead of having a man come in two or three years from now saying, "Such and such a thing happened. I was stripped to the waist and examined; out I went, and nobody looked at me to make any notes of how I was." The examination does take a considerably longer time than formerly; they have specialists and so on, as my hon. friend knows.
In my judgment, however, there is no reason for these men being kept at our depots for any long time, except that of course medical officers are none too plentiful, and they tell me that a board can only handle properly something like fifteen men a day. So that it takes a number of boards if you have to deal with three, four, five or six hundred men, or perhaps a thousand or more as they may have at Halifax. It does take time to get them out, but I really think that is principally due to the necessity of taking time in order to see that the examination is properly carried out. As a matter of fact, we are putting someone in charge of all these depots, having him go around to see if he cannot smarten up the procedure. I know one depot in particular which is extremely efficient. We have had officers in command of other depots visit this one to see how it is run, and they have worked out something in the nature of a belt-line procedure.
There is another thought that has just come to me. We had an investigation made of our examination system, our reception system and our discharge system by officers of the United States army, and I must say that the result put our people very much on their toes. Perhaps they became a bit complacent following the compliments they received from these visiting officers because of the care that was taken in connection with the discharge of personnel. I remember writing a memorandum at the time congratulating them on the record they had made, but adding that I hoped this would not lead to complacency. Coming back to my hon. friend's statement, I say that by all means these men ought to be out of the army. We try to work just as hard as we can, in order to get them out just as quickly as we can, and the procedure is being improved just as much as it possible can, always having in mind the examinations which are required in order that pension cases may not arise in the future, and that men may not be deprived of evidence which they would have had if they had undergone a proper examination.

Recently I have had brought to my attention several cases similar to those referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. The complaint I hear is that these men get tired of hanging around and apply for their discharge. Invariably the discharge is given, but then these men are barred from receiving the one month's pay and the clothing allowance. For instance, I have before me a letter from the Edmonton branch of the legion-

accept civilian employment?

Let me read part of the letter:
I think this is one of the grievances that certainly should be rectified, as men who have been overseas and are returned to this country certainly get fed up hanging around not doing anything, and they naturally after a time make application for discharge, which is inevitably granted.
Then, due to the fact that the discharge was granted: at his own request, the man is refused his one month's pay and the clothing allowance. I have referred these cases to the department but so far have received no reply. It does seem to me that when a man has been overseas for two or three years and returns to this country he should be granted a discharge and should be eligible to receive the one month's pay and the clothing allowance.

Would my hon. friend mind giving me one name?

I am referring to the case of Corporal J. R. Wallace, and also the case of Private Jossul. I believe in the latter case, however, the allowance has been granted, though at the time the letter was written it had not. Of the four oases referred to in this letter, the allowance was granted in only one.
What was the second name?

The first case is that of Corporal J. R. Wallace, No. R-93837. The second case is that of Private Jossul, but in that case I believe the allowance has been granted, because there is a postscript to the letter which reads:
I am very pleased to let you know that_ I have been successful in having Jossul's rehabilitation granted, so maybe the others will come through.
